summary: The assessee was assessed to wealth tax for the assessment years 1965 66, 1966 67 and 1967 68. The Wealth Tax Officer included a sum of Rs. 1,50,000 estimated as the accrued interest on the assessee 's money lending investments. The assessee appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and urged that as it maintained its books of account in accordance with the cash system of accounting the accrued interests on the money lending investment could not be included in the wealth tax assessments. The Appellate Tribunal held that the judgment of the Orissa High Court was binding on it, and that the view taken by the Orissa high Court was correct. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The concept of valuation date in terms of the last day of a period which is also the relevant period under the Income Tax Act, 1961, as the valuation date. [310F] (2) The scheme of the Wealth Tax Act shows that broadly Parliament has fixed upon the last date of the previous year, as defined under the Act, as to what accrues as a right also falls to be included within the assets of an assessee under the Wealth tax Act. That being so, the conclusion is inescapable that even though the accounts of the assessee are maintained on cash basis interest due on accrual basis, though not realised, on the outstandings of the money lent investments could not he included in its net wealth of the asses see under the wealth Tax Act. [309F G] (3) The computation of the net wealth is correct and the conclusion was inescapable that the assets to be considered are not circumscribed by any consideration of the particular system of accounts adopted by the assessee. [311G H] Vedreva Venkappa Rao vs Commissioner of Wealth tax, ; , followed.

The respondent, a Time Keeper in the Department of preparing pay bills and other bills of work charg ing under the Punjab Government Servants (Conduct) Rules 1966, was appointed as Inquiry Officer. The Inquiry Officer framed charges against the respondent. In the inquiry report, the Inquiry Officer found that he had entered the name of Ashok Kumar in the pay roll for May 1969 and that he was a member of the staff of the Department. He also found him guilty of entering the name in the service register for May 1970 or that it was his duty to prepare the list. The respondent filed an appeal before the Central Administrative Tribunal, which dismissed the same on the ground that the punishment awarded to him was disproportionate to the delinquency of the respondent and was in stark contrast to the punishment imposed upon him. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that (i) the respondent had entered into the name o f Ashok Kumar as his own brother and that there were others too, and as such he should not be allowed to take advantage of the penalty imposed by the disciplinary authority on the basis of some of the findings of the Inquiry officer; (ii) the Tribunal was wrong in directing the Governor of Orissa to reconsider the penalty awarded to the respondent when the findings recorded as to h is misdemeanour were supported by legal evidence. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Tribunal has no power to interfere with the penalty on the grounds that it is not commensurate with the delinquence of the official. It is appropriate to rema nise the order of the Tribunal imposing a lesser penalty on a delinquent officer. [27C] 1.2 In the instant case, the respondent was not offered a reasonable opportunity to defend himself and accordingly the enquiry and consequential ord er of dismissal were found to be bad. The Tribunal had no power under section 27(1) of the Act to impose any punishment to meet the ends of justice. Where the person without enquiry is dis pute guilty, removed or reduced in rank solely on the view that he would have weighed with the authority in dismissing the public servant, the Tribunal has jurisdiction to exercise its power of review subject to the court permitting it. If the penalty can lawfully be imposed and is imposed on the proved misconduct, the tribunal has no pow er to substitute its own discretion for that of the authority. [28D E] 1:3 The Tribunal was in error in directing that the Governor should reconsider the matter. [29F] 2.1 In the present case, there was no doubt that the respondent did not have entered the service of the department or had been working in his Division. He was only otherwise dealt with und er the Government Servants ' (Conduct ) Rules which are applicable to him. The disciplinary authority must however bear in mind that the Tribunal is just a substitute to t he civil court and High Court has no jurisdiction to interfere. [30G H] 2:2 In view of the principles to which we have call ed, the order imposing a higher penalty on respondent cannot be sustained. [31A B] 2 :3 The disciplinary proceedings are not vitiated by any legal or valid reasons. The punishment imposed is too severe and it is just and proper that the penalty should be reduced in its discretion to be imposed. If there has been an enquiry, the penalty would be vitiated and the order based on such enquiry would be justified having regard to the misdemeanour established. [32B C] 2(a) In the case of proceedings under section 10 of the , the Tribunal could not substitute its decision with the findings arrived at by the Inquiry Officers or the competent authority. The adequacy of penalty unless it is malafide is a matter exclusively within the jurisdiction of the compete nt authority. If, however, the findings are based on evidence even if some of it is found to have been irrelevant or extraneous to the matter, the Court has power to exercise that power to re examine the penalty.

The appellants were the legal representatives of one of the deceased plaintiff. The suit was dismissed on the ground that he was not in possession of the suit property and, therefore, a decree for eviction could not be passed against him. The respondents filed an application under Order 2 Rule 2(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure praying for restoration of possession on the grounds that the appellant was a lessee in respect of seven lots on an annual rent of Rs. 3600 payable in advance in three instalments; that he had paid the rent upto the end of December 1967 and that the first installment of 1968 but the owner, defendant No. 2, in collusion with defendant No 1 executed a deed of lease in favour of the latter effective from January 1, 1968 on the strength whereof defendant No 2 was in possession and that he has not been dispossessed; that the suit was barred by res judicata as well as constructive res judicata because the plaintiff was not a tenant or deemed tenant. The Trial Court upheld the plaintiffs contention and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that since the plaintiff had in fact been dispossessed, there was no question of granting an injunction and/or constructive resjudicata as found by the Trial Court; that even after the Fifth Amendment came into force the plaintiff has not applied to the Mamlatdar for possession of land within the period allowed by section 18 of the Act and had therefore, allowed the first defendant to become a deemed purchaser of the land in question on the basis of his tenancy. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in holding that the plaintiff came to court contending that even though his lease was not terminated as provided by section 9 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, he was a trespasser in the property and was liable to be evicted therefrom. [1020C] 1.2 The High Courts were right in observing that it would be just and fair that the issue whether defendant No1 was a tenant in respect Of the land is not based on the allegation that the possession of his predecessor was forcibly taken sometime in the second week of June, 1968. The question whether defendant 1 was a 'tenant ' or a deemed tenant was essentially one of fact. [1120E] 1:3. Section 7 of the said Act provides that if any question arises whether any person is a tenant, or should be deemed to be a tenant under the Act, the Mamlatdar shall decide such question. The jurisdiction of the civil court is specifically barred by sub section (2) of section 58 from settling, deciding or dealing with any question which is by or under the provisions of the . [1121F] 1 :4. Section 8(2) provides that no Court shall have jurisdiction to settle, decide or deal with any questions which is, by or u/s 4, sub section 2, or (iii) the Civil Court may pass an order directing the parties to maintain their rights in respect thereof. [1221G] 1 5. Section 9(2)(a) provides for a person who has been evicted from the land on or after 1st July 1962 and such person is entitled to recover immediate possession of that land in the manner prescribed by orunder the Act unless it is shown that his tenancy was terminated in the year 1966. [1321A] 6. Section 29(2), which provides that a person shall be deemed not to be tenant under sub section 4, does not debar him from deciding even incidentally questions failing within the ambit of section 7 of Act or (3) the civil Court has jurisdiction to decide the question regarding tenancy on merits and it is open to the Civil court to consider passing a decree in eviction but if on the other hand he is held to be tenants, the Civil Courts may consider passing of a decree. [1421B C] 7. Section 10(2).

The petitioners are employed as daily rated employees. They were paid minimum wages prescribed by the Deputy Commissioner for like categories of workmen. They filed writ petitions in this Court challenging their claim. The High Court allowed the petition holding that the principle of "equal pay for equal work" is not one of the fundamental rights expressly guaranteed by Article 14 of the Constitution and that it is open to the State to classify employees on the basis of qualifications, duties and responsibilities of the posts concerned. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the Corporation has no regularly employed carpenters; that the petitioners are paid the minimum wages admissible to them under the Bonus Act and provident fund benefits under the Employees ' Provident Fund Act. Dismissing the writ petitions, HELD: 1. The principle of equal pay for Equal work is not a permissible exercise normally. It is open for the State Government to classify employ ees on the based on merit with due regard to experience and seniority. It cannot be evaluated by the mere averments in the self serving affidavits or counter affidavits of the parties. It must be left to be evaluated and determined by expert body. The principal claim of the peti tioners therefore fails and is rejected. [667B C] 2.1 The principle laid down in Federation of All India Customs and Central Excise Stenographers (Recognised) vs Union of India, ; at 245, is not applicable to the instant case because the petitioners were carpenter; better called as craftsmen. By the general description of their job, one cannot come to the conclusion that every carpenter or craftsman is equal to the other in the performance of his work. The two jobs by the merely ipse dixit of the volume or by the volume of work performed cannot be rated as equal. It was not just a comparison of physical activity. It requires the consideration of various dimensions of the job. The accuracy required by the job and the dexterity it entails may differ from job to job. It can be evaluated, by expert bodies. [668C D] 2:2 In the instant cases, the petitioners have been treated as construction workers and they are being paid the wages admissible under the Labour Act. They cannot enforce the right to "equal wages for equal Work". The discrimination complained of must be within the same estab lishment owned by the same management. A comparison cannot be made with counterparts in other establishments with different management, or even in establishments in different geographical proximity though owned by them unless it is shown that there is a discrimination amongst the same set of employees by the similar employer unless it was shown that the same sets of employees are comparable with the counterparts In other establishments. [669C D; 670A B] 2 :3 The petitioners are carpentants and better called " crafts men". By the General description of the work, one could come to their conclusion that each carpenter, one can come to them their rights elsewhere in accordance with law applicable to them.

The appellant was convicted and sentenced to death by the Sessions Judge, for murder of one Malan. The High Court acquitted him but convicted him under section 302 read with section 120B I.P.C. and sentenced him to imprisonment for life. On appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the conviction of the accused alone for conspiracy under section 120A I. P.C., is unsustainable in law as at least two persons are required for an offence of conspiracy under Section 120A IPC and he relied upon a decision of this Court in Topandas vs State of Bombay, ; , which held that the appellant 's conviction and sentence awarded to him were not sustainable in law because at least 2 persons were required for the offence of criminal conspiracy under s.120A I P. C. and he had been rightly convicted and acquitted by the High Court. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The retracted judicial confession of accused 5 could not be relied upon against accused 6 in view of the fact that accused 6 who had been tried along with accused 5 had been acquitted by a trial court of charge No. 1 framed under section 307 read with s. 120B IPC and accused 5 was not charged for the offences of murder of Malan, and acquitted accused 5 and directed him to be set at liberty forthwith and dismissed Criminal Appeal 38 of 1977 filed against that acquittal which was filed only against accused 2, 3, 4 and 7. [785C D] 2. The appellant had been convicted under section 201 read with Section 120B of I.p.C and sentenced for life imprisonment by the trial court. He had been wrongly convicted and convicted under s 302 readwith section 120 B I.Ps. and section 120(B I P C. [788E F] 3. In view of this technical flaw that the retracted judicial confessions of accused Nos. 5 and 6 were not reliable, the conviction and sentences awarded to them by the courts below are set aside and they are acquitted.

The appellant, who was the sole executor of the will executed by his father, filed a suit for possession of certain properties in dispute and a declaration that the said properties were his absolute property. The trial court decreed the suit but on appeal the High Court held that the will was not proved to be the last will and testament of the testator and that it was not genuine or valid and that the appellant had failed to prove that the money for the purchase of items 3, 4 and 5 came out of any bequest under the will. The High Court also held that even if it had been established that the testator had executed the will in favour of his father he was entitled to a life interest in items 1, 2 and 3 and accordingly decreed the appellant 's suit for recovery of possession against respondent No. 1. On appeal by certificate, Held, that the High court was in error in coming to the conclusion that it could not be said that the execution of the Will was proved to have been duly proved. The will was a registered one and had been executed by the testator on the same day. It was not a genuine document and the appellant was entitled under section 3, of the Indian Succession Act to claim possession of the properties covered by the will and as such he had failed in proving that the property was the last Will of the deceased. Parker vs Felgund (I.L.R. , approved. The question whether a will executed in favour is proved to the satisfaction of the Court must inevitably depend on the circumstances of each case. In the present case, the High Courts were not justified in recording its findings on two other issues in the present appeal.

The appellant company was carrying on business of sale and sale of Arcotors, known as "Cinema Arc Carbons" manufactured by the appellant company. The goods were purchased by persons other than those who ran cinemas or for any other use. Of course, it was very difficult to identify a taxable commodity merely by the use to which it may be put. The Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal held that the common or ordinary use of the are carbons was that they exuded their power foul light cast, through the projectors on cinema screens and sound recording and reproducing equipment lenses films and parts and accents in a particular area. It also found that the sales tax authorities were compelled to consider the use which is generally made of the arc carbins. The High Court held that these were not taxable under Entry 41 of the First Schedule to the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1957. Dismissing the appeals by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. The term "accessories" is used in the schedule to describe goods which may have been manufactured for use as an aid or addition. A sense in which the word accessory is used is given in Webster 's Third New International Dictionary as follows: "all objects or device that is not essential in itself but that adds to the beauty, convenience, or effectiveness of something else". [562 E] 2. The definition of "accessory" is not exhaustive in which it occurs in a schedule in which description of goods to be taxed indicate that the expression "required for use there with" has been employed for equipment or accessories connected with the main purpose. For instance, in entry No. 4 of Schedule 1 of the Madras General Sales tax Act, the words "parts thereof" are used in several entries, such as entry No 6 for clocks, time pieces and watches, entry No 11 for dictaphones and other similar apparatus for recording sound, and entry No 12 for dictating, stage lighting, or where powerful lighting for photography or other purposes may be required, could not detract from the classification to which the carbon are belong. That is determined by their ordinary or commonly known purpose or user. [562 F G] 3. The expression "part" in Entry 41 means that the words used therein include goods as are ordinarily also used for other purposes than as (1) (1965) 16 S.T.C. 862, 966. (2) (1970) 26 S. T.C., 87. (3) (70 I.A. 129) and (4) (1971) 27 S.C . 45.

The petitioners in these petitions are the owners of a quarry lease or any other mineral concession granted under the Rules. The petitioners in their writ petition challenged the validity of Rule 21 as it existed prior to the issue of the notification dated June 18, 1981 issued by the State Government under section 15 of the Act amending the Gujarat Minor Mineral Rules 1966 with regard to the grant of royalty in respect of minor minerals. They also challenged the constitutional validity of rule 21 as being violative of Article 301 of the Constitution. The High Court struck down Rule 21 on the ground that it was discriminatory and violative of Articles 14, 19(1)(g) and 31(2). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that (i) the royalty levied and covered under the rules should be applied only for mineral development and not for other purposes; (ii) Rule 21 which was substituted by the issue in 1981 was discriminatory in character, and (iii) Rule 33 C was violative of article 14. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The levy is made under a law made by the Central Government. It is not an imposition made by a law making authority on which alone the restriction contemplat ed under Article 304(b) applies. [412C] 2.1 Rule 21 is valid and does not offend Article 14 provided the classification is a reasonable one. The State Government is entitled to grant concessions and exemptions wherever necessary having regard to its purpose of the statute, the levy of royalty is incidental to the regulation and development of minerals. [413D E] 2:2 In view of the constitutional policy underlying the Constitution if a concession is shown in favour of the poor and the down trodden, it cannot be said that there was no reasonable nexus between the classification for purposes of the proviso to rule 21 to show concession in the matter of payment of royalty and social policy underlying Article 304 (b) of the constitution. [414F G] 2(i) The levy of royalties is incidental or ancillary to the regulations and development, of minerals, and therefore, it does not mean that the said tax should be used only for development of mineral and not any other purpose sanctioned by law. [416A B] (ii). Rule 21 has no application to the present case because the levy is in the nature of a tax and it was not in the form of fee which could be used by the Government for any purpose. The Rules are therefore ultra vires the State Legislature. [411C D] 2.(iii) The Act under the Act was made for purposes other than those specified in Rule 21, whereas the mining lease may be given to persons mentioned in rule 9. Under Rule 18 of the Rules the period of lease in case of a minor mineral can be for a much longer period, it can be upto 10 years in respect thereof. The period or land covered by a mining lease is governed by rule 15 which says that no quarry lease shall be granted for an area exceeding 10 hectares in case there is any other minerals. Rule 33 B provides that the competent officer may notify areas of limestone, Black Trap and sand stone quarries in re spect of minor mineral. The notification under the said rule was made on June 18. 1981 and the rules were amended by the Gujarat Mineral Rules, 1966. Rule 21 was substituted in place of the former rule 21. The new rule 21 was introduced in 1981. Rule 22 provides that no royalty shall be payable for an Area exceeding 10 per cent of the royalty payable by the lessee and no royalty is payable by village potters who manufacture upto one lakh bricks per year. Rule 23 B provides for a renewal of quarrying Parwana on payment of a fee of Rs.7 per metric tonne. The rule also provides that in case the concession is not granted, the State may grant such Parwana in the same way as it may require.

The appellant was elected as a trustee by the Sengunatha Mudaliars of Manjakollai village in the District of Nagapattinam. The appellant challenged the election on the ground that the trusteeship of the temple was not hereditary and that the suit was not barred by limitation. The High Court allowed the appeal, set aside the judgment of the Subordinate Judge and restored the decree of the trial court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the succession is "regulated by usage" and therefore the office of a hereditary trustee is in the nature of property. HELD: (i) The word "succession" in relation to property and rights and interests in property generally implies "passing of an interest from one person to another". [426 B] (ii)The expression "regulated" in section 6(9) must be construed along with the phrase "sucession to this office" and when so construed that part of the definition would only apply where the ordinary rules of succession under the Hindu law are modified by usage and succession has to be determined in accordance with the modified rules. The word 'successor ' in relation,to property and right means the trustee of a religious institution. [425 C D] (iii)The words "regulatedby usage" in s 6(1)(c) must mean their normal rules of inheritance under the Indian law are modification of Hindu Law by usage. In the present case, there is no warrant for this argument. The phrase "regulated ' in section six(9), does not mean a hereditary trust or the office to which he has been appointed.

The prosecution case against the appellant was that he along with two others, armed with a knife and a knife, had killed one of them. The deceased was sleeping on a bench outside his cattle shed in the open space which is shown in the site plan (exhibit P15). He got up and saw the accused hitting him with knife. He got down and saw two persons running ahead of him. He ran to his elder brother who was sleeping near him. When he went near him, he was already dead. The appellant was declared absconder. On hearing a noise, the deceased came out and saw one person lying on the ground with knife and another with knife, and that he had bleeding injuries on several parts of his body. A crowd gathered and witnessed the incident. He also saw two other persons running towards the place where the deceased was sitting. The younger brother of the deceased who was a lepered brother was running after stabbing him with a dagger. He was also seen by the deceased when he went to the scene of occurrence. He had bleeding injury on several part of his dead body. The High Court acquitted the second accused, Jabamani Nadar alias Kanyakumari Comrade alias Ramu and convicted him under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced him to death. On appeal by special leave, the appellant contended that the testimony of PW 4 in so far as he implicated the second appellant was not reliable because he had no motive to implicate the first accused; that there has been a history of a bitter feud spanning over nearly a decade between the first and the deceased; that the High Court erred in convicting the second respondent on the sole testimony of a single witness. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The evidence of PW4 is not reliable as he was declared absent from behind. It is clear that there were more than one assailant and yet for the FIR it appears that there was only one assailant. This may not, in a given case, be considered as a very serious infirmity since the witness may not have seen the other. assailants when he came running to the place of occurrence; but the fact that the witness has stated in the first information report that the deceased had been only mentioning the name of accused makes it doubtful if the crowd had gathered at the place. The fact that this eye witness could be persuaded to substitute PWs 1, 2 and 3 for his deceased brother as chasing the assailants, degrades him from the status of an absolutely reliable witness. He is certainly an obliging witness and cannot at all be trustworthy. This witness may also not have a quali fied evidence in implicating the accused for the mere asking by someone, if not by the inimical police officer (PW 23) against whom criminal cases were pending at the instance of the accused 's father. Apart from that there is no other assailants who arrived at the scene. [711E F] 2. The prosecution case was that the appellant along with three others attacked PW 4 and PW 5 on the same boat with knife which he had stabbed him. The first information Report was very close to the site of occurrence within about 15 minutes of the occurrence. It was also mentioned in the First Information Report that the first deceased chased the accused as the latter was running away after stabbing the appellant with knife 's knife. The second report was lodged at the Thana which is very close and the same day. There were also no blood stains on the bench where he was said to have been stabbed. It may be that these two witnesses had stated in their first information reports that the accused was only mentioning his name as his assailant, this earlier version appears to be contradicted by the medical evidence. [612E F; 710A B] 3.

The assessee was a partner in a firm of solicitors. The firm was carried on by the firm as its managing agents and the realisations were to be divided amongst the partners. The business was carried out by the firms. The assessee was carrying on the business of carrying on business in the names of Amarchand and Amarchand. The Income tax Officer sought to tax these realisations. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the amounts received after the death of Amar Chand were not liable to income tax as they were not income of the Hindu undivided family but merely represented inheritance or realisations of the assets of Amarachand. The Tribunal, however, held that though for different reasons the amounts which were received by the heirs and legal representatives of Amarichand were not taxable, the amount was assessable under section 24B of the Income tax Act. On appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the amounts in question were not exempt from income tax in view of the provisions of section 24 B of the Act; (2) the amount which were sought to be taxed and which had been held not to be liable to tax as received by Amarchand, and (3) the assessee was entitled to claim that the said amounts were not assessable to income Tax. HELD : (i) The amounts which are sought to have been taxed and who are not liable for payment of income tax are those which were not received in the previous year and are therefore not liable under section 23B of Income tax. [707 B] (ii) The provisions of s 24B do not extend to tax liability of the estate of a deceased person beyond the previous or the account year in which that person dies. In the present case the amounts were sought by the assessee to be assessed and which have been held by him as income received by him before his death and therefore they are not taxable under section 12B. [608 C D] (iii) The amount which are claimed to have become liable to Income tax in regard to those years cannot be called income received in tho previous year. [700 E F] (iv) The High Court rightly answered the question in the negative and against the Commissioner of Income Tax.

The petitioners were appointed between December 27, 1956 and July 4, 1968. They challenged the Act as ultra vires the Constitution on the ground that article 16(3) of the Constitution was violated by the provisions of article 16 (b). The High Court held that article 3(1) did not apply to the case and quashed the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the petitioners that the power conferred by section 3 of the Public Employment (Requirement as to Residence) Act, 1957, was a valid law prescribing the requirement as to residence in a particular part of the State and that the provisions were ultra vires. HELD : The contention must be negatived. Article 16(b) does not require any discrimination among other things on the grounds of residence. Realising this that sometimes local sentiments may have to be respected or sometimes an inroad from more advance States into less developed States may have been to be prevented and a residential qualification may, therefore, have to he prescribed, the exception in clause (3) was made applicable to the State of Andhra Pradesh. [121 E F] The words "residence within the State" in article 16 are controlled by the words 'residence ' or its duration rather than its location within the state. The word 'State ' here is not controlled by any other name but it must be understood in the extended use given to it by the definition of that word article 12. [122 G H] In the present case, the petitioners were employed between December 26, 1956, and July 1, 1968, and therefore, they could not claim to be a citizen under article 16 of the .

The appellant was a postman attached to the Bulandshahr Post office. He was tried for offences under section 52 of the Indian Post Office Act, 1898 and in two of them also for offences punishable under sections 467 and 471 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The trial court acquitted him but on appeal the High Court held that the appellant had secreted the five registered letters in question and on this finding set aside his acquittal and convicted him in each of the three appeals. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that (1) the search was illegal inasmuch as it was in contravention of section 103 of the Evidence Act, (2) the seizure of the articles was not vitiated by any irregularity or illegality; (3) the conviction having been based on circumstantial evidence the High court had no jurisdiction to set aside the acquittal and convict him in respect of offences under sections 466 and 471. HELD : (i) The mere fact that there is even a delay of several months in delivering a postal article to the addressee would not mean that the article had ceased to be in course of transmission by post. [415 D] (ii)The mere fact of possession does not suffice to show that the articles were delivered to the addressees. The presumption under section 103 is that the goods are delivered to them. It has not been found that they have been secreted by the appellant. Therefore, the conviction cannot be sustained. [416 G H] (iii)The search was in the exclusive possession of the appellant and there was no evidence that it was ever with him. The mere circumstance that there was even a lapse of several years in delivering the postal article did not suffice for holding that he had secreting the articles.

The appellant, a public servant, filed a complaint before the Nyaya Panchayat alleging that he had been abused and assaulted by the respondent. The Magistrate ordered investigation of the case and submitted a report to the High Court. The High Court admitted the application and stayed further proceedings before the magistrate. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The High court was not justified in interfering with the order of the Single Judge. The mere fact that the Magistrate wanted to avoid the petitioner 's affidavit being brought on record by declaring him guilty would not be sufficient to give him an opportunity to accept the mere statement of the party that the High court had stayed proceedings before it. (ii) In such matters those who assert that a person had knowledge of the order must prove this fact beyond all reasonable doubt. If there is any doubt, the benefit ought to be given to the person charged with contempt of Court. If a person bona fide comes to the conclusion on the material placed before him that the source of information is not authentic he cannot be held guilty of contempt of court for disobeying the order. The question then arises whether the Sarpanch and the Pan chas had knowledge about the existence of the orders of the High Courts dated December 20, 1963. The only material before them was the application dated December 25, 1963 which was not supported by any affidavit sworn to before a person authorised to administer oaths.

The appellant was convicted of the offence under section 302, I.P.C., by the Sessions Judge, Etawah, for causing the death of Sheo Sahai and sentenced to death. The High Court acquitted the appellant on the ground that the entire report dictated by him was inadmissible in evidence as its contents amounted to a confession of the accused. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Court was wrong in rejecting the statement of the appellant as inadmissible in his evidence, because, the evidence relied upon by the High court was insufficient to establish that the appellant had murdered Sheo Sahai. HELD : (i) The conviction of the appellants under section 307 I. P.C. must be set aside and they should be sentenced to imprisonment for life. [206 B] (ii) The extra judicial confession of an accused is not normally considered with favour but that does not mean that such a confession coming from a person who has no reason to state falsely and to whom it is made in circumstances which tend to support his statement, should not be believed. The murder was committed in the month of June. Both on account of the temperature and on account Of the culprit 's desire to wash of blood marks on his person, the appellant 's bathing in the Canal at that hour of the night cannot be said to have been improbable. [207 C D] (iii) The High court erred in rejecting a statement of an approver as inadmissible under section 25 of the Evidence Act. It was not stated by sub Inspector Kishan Singh, nor it was alleged that the confession made to him was false. The evidence of the approver was corroborated by the evidence of other prosecution witnesses whose testimony had been rightly accepted by the trial court. [208 E F] (iv) The evidence led by the prosecution consisted of the evidence relating to motive and purchase of a sword, which has not been normally considered in the circumstances of this case. It is not necessary that such an inference should be drawn from the facts that the accused had committed the murder. The conviction was therefore bad.

The respondent No. 1, a local authority, filed an election petition challenging the validity of the electoral roll on the ground that the entire election process had become vitiated on account of the defect in the notice issued under Rule 4(1) of the Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, 1956 (No. 23 of 1956). The Election Tribunal dismissed the petition holding that the respondent No 1 was not prompt in moving the High Court and that the petitioner did not have any objection to the inclusion of his name in the electoral rolls on October 19, 1978. On appeal by special leave, the High court held that respondent No 2 had asked for a further direction to be issued to the respondents to refrain from conducting the poll on December 31, 1978, and directed the issue of notice of the petition and stay application to the Respondents and issued an interim order directing the respondents not to notify the results of the election under Rule 46 of the Rules. The High Court also held that the writ petition was rightly dismissed by the High Courts as there was no satisfactory explanation for the delay in filing the petition. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that since the period of 20 days had been fixed for entertaining claims and objections, a large number or people who could have filed claims and objection were prevented from preferring them within 30 days from the date of publication of the notice under Rule 3(1), the High Commission had no jurisdiction to do so. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The power of the High 'Court under Article 226 of the Constitution to issue an appropriate writ is discretionary and if the High, prima facie, is satisfied that there is not satisfactory explanation far the inordinate delay, it may reject the petition if it finds that the issue has been brought to its notice by the petitioners immediately after it was noticed by them. [497G H] 2. The powers of the Court under Article 227 of the constitution to issue any appropriate writ are discretionary and when the High/Court finds that there has not been satisfactory explanation, it is reject ed. The final electoral roll was published on November 16, 1978 and it was notified that the nominations could be filed on and after November 25, 1978 but before December 25,1978, a few days thereafter, for the first time that a letter was addressed by petitioner No. 6 to the Collector drawing his attention to the error that had crept into the notice published under Rule 5(1). The writ petition itself was filed on December 28, 1978 for the second time that the names of 34 persons were received by the Deputy Collector and that was rejected by the authorities concerned. [498A B] 3. In view of the fact that the period mentioned in the notices issued under rule 4( 1) of Madhya Pradesh Munici pal Corporation (Preparation, Revision and Publication) Rules, 1963 has been adjourned twice before, it cannot be said that there was any satisfactory explanation from the petitioners for the inordinate delayed filing of the writ petitions.

The appellant was the director of a company and its directors were prosecuted for failure to comply with the provisions of section 220(1) of the Companies Act, 1913. The High Court held that if no general body meeting had been held and the balance sheet and profit and loss account had not been laid before a general body, there could be no question of that balance sheet not being adopted nor of complying with the requirements of section 132 and that the appellant was guilty of an offence under section 134(4). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the principle accepted by this Court in Park vs Lawton, ; , that a company or its directors in a prosecution under section 32 and section 133 of the 1913 Act could not in defence to such prosecution rely upon their own failure to call the general body meetings as a defence to the prosecution; (2) the principles laid down in Park 's case were not applicable to the present case, and (3) the appellant had been guilty of offences under sections 76 and 133 of 1956. HELD : (i) The High Courts have taken a similar view and have held that the principle is consistent with the principle embodied in Park v Lawton; , and (ii) the provisions unmistakably indicate, as they are clearly clear, that the holding of the annual general meeting and the laying before it of the balance sheets and profit & loss account was a sine qua non for filing of the copies thereof before the Registrar. If no general Body meeting is held, the persons concerned cannot be said to have committed a default in complying with those provisions. [415 D E] (iii) The appellant had not taken any objection to call a general meeting as a prosecution witness and that there was no failure to calling a general election meeting. [416 G H] (iv) The principle accepted in Park V Lawton 's Case is that the requirement of section 134 of the Act is that this section should be interpreted in the light of the law made by Parliament and not on the necessity of their being laid before the general meeting of the company not being fulfilled. [414 C D] (v) The provisions unmistakably indicated, as it was, that if the balance Sheet is not adopted at the general meetings before which it is laid, a statement of that fact and of the reasons therefore have to be annexed to the balance Sheets and profit or loss account, as the case may be, would be made punishable under sub section (4) of that section. [413 D E; 414 C] (vi) The provision in Park was not consistent with section 132 of the 1956 Act and the failure to reach any one of the stages within the time prescribed is made penal by the Act. [411 G H, 413 A] (vii) The contention that the provisions in sections 32 and 134 of 1956 were not complied with by the appellant as they did not comply with those sections cannot be accepted. [409 C D].

The respondent was charged with offences under sections 3 and 5 of the West Bengal Special Courts Ordinance, 1949, which was replaced by the West Benabari Act, 1950. The trial commenced on August 9, 1951, and the accused were convicted and sentenced to varying terms of imprisonment by the Special Court. On appeal the High Court held that section 5(1) of the Act had no application to the case as it did not provide for a speedier trial but only provided for the trial by a special court and did not make any distinction between offences under section 3 and those under section 5. The State appealed to this Court with certificate. Held, that the classification made in section 5 (1) was valid and the classification must be held to be reasonable. The classification must not be arbitrary but must be based on some qualities or characteristics which are peculiar to persons or who are left out but those qualities or attributes must have a reasonable relation to the object of the legislation. The distinction between the two classes of offences is, therefore, well established and that in each case judges must look straight into the heart of things and regard the facts of each case concretely much as a jury would do; and yet not quite as a result of the enactment of the law itself. The appellant was appointed as a Lecturer in Radiology in Maulana Azad Medical College, New Delhi. He was later promoted to the post of Associate Professor of Radiotherapy in the Medical College. The post of Professor of radiology in the medical college was a post belonging to the Central Health Service and continued to work in that capacity till October 8, 1964. By an order dated January 1, 1965, the Government of India, Ministry of Health, Health & Family Planning Department of Health by its letter dated April 6, 1965 directed that the appellant could not be considered for appointment to the said post as he did not possess at least five years ' teaching experience as Reader/Assistant Professor in the concerned speciality. The appellant was not only holding the post as an Associate Professor but also performing the duties attached to the teaching post of Radiologist. He filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order dated April6, 1965 and the order of the Central Government dated January 17, 1976. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal by special leave it was contended that the post was divided into two classes viz., Class I and Class II and the appellant was also performing his duties as an Assistant Professor of Pathology in a medical college and treated as an assistant Professor of P Associate Professor in that Department. It was further submitted that the teaching experience gained by him while holding the said posts was different and the post could not he taken into consideration for determining his eligibility for appointment as Associate Professor. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The appellant could be considered to have been appointed to the Post of Associate professor in Ma reciprocology in Malulana Azad medical College, which had fallen vacant in 1973. As a necessary consequence, it was eligible to be considered by the Union Public Service Commission for appointment of Assistant Professor as Associate Professors of Radiological Institute in Mahammed Azad Medical college. [8E F] 1.2 The Ministry of Finance, Department of Revenue, New South Wales, has been using the Central Excise and Taxation Commissioner 's Office Manuals of the Government for the purpose of reorganising the service into five categories viz., Categories I, C, D, E, E and E. The said office does not make him eligible for appointment in the post. If the appellant is eligible to hold the post he can always apply irrespective of the fact whether or not he is in the line of promotion. It is for the Union Government to advertise the post in the manner provided by r. That being so, the appellant who was a highly qualified person and has the requisite teaching experience, as Radiologist cum Associate Professor, of Radiology (ex officio) in the Irwin Hospital, could be appointed by direct recruitment from amongst persons holding the posts of Associate Professors or Assistant Professor in any medical college or teaching institution from Grade I and Grade II. [88G H; 89A] 2.1 It is not for the Court to give the appellant promotion or make his appointment to a post of Assistant Director of Radiologists in Mahammad Azad Medical Colleges. The Ministry 's letter dated January 25, 1982 addressed to the Secretary (Medical), Delhi Administration that the said office of Professor in Manaecology (Ex officio) will be abolished with effect from October 9, 1964 cannot be taken into account. It may be pointed out that the Ministry of Education has been utilizing his services as such for teaching the post graduate and under graduate students of the Maulana Nehru Medical College for the Municiological Department of studies for the academic year 1966 65. [89F G] 2:2 The appellant, while holding a non teaching post in a teaching hospital like the Irin Azad Medical Institute, was not holding the Post as an associate Professor ofika Radiology and he had the requisite research experience as Radiologists cum Associate Professors in the said institution.

The appellant company had taken on lease a piece of land for the purpose of manufacturing tea. The workmen were paid minimum wages and this was covered by item 2 of the Schedule attached to the Order of reference. The Company made an application under section 10(1) (d) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, for adjudication by the Tribunal. The Tribunal held that there was no identical industry in the region comparable with the company and therefore, the workmen were entitled to bonus on any further rise in price index. On appeal by the workmen it was contended before this Court that the Tribunal had committed an error of law in not making calculation of surplus available on the basis of the Full Bench Formula approved by this Court in French Motor Car Co. Ltd. vs The Workmen, ; , and that the principle laid down by this court in French Motors (India) Ltd. case was applicable to the present case. HELD: (i) The Tribunal had not committed any error of fact or law requiring interference by this tribunal. [674 E] In the instant case, the Tribunal committed an apparent error in arriving at its decision and consequently the total minimum wage packet of a workman in the company should be fixed at Rs. 95. This was done on the assumption that the minimum wage fixed by the appellant company was not uniform throughout the period of 5 years. [678 F] (ii) The finding of fact recorded by the Industrial Tribunal is correct and must be upheld. [677 G H] French Motor car Co. vs Its Workmen, , referred to. (iii) The award had to cover the year 1963 64 also and at least for that year the accounts could not possibly have been completed as that year was still running when the award was given by the tribunal on the 11th January, 1964. [676 G] (iv) The appellant company is paying profit bonus equivalent to three months ' basic wage of each workman.

The appellant, a partnership firm, had been assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1960 61. The Income tax Officer, Ward A, assessed the appellant 's income under section 148 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1961. The appellant challenged the validity of that notice as well as proceedings taken on the strength of that notices on various grounds. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the impugned notice was invalid inasmuch as it did not comply with the requirements of section 151(2) of the Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Income Tax Officer had no material before him which could satisfy the requirements under either cl. (a) or cl.(b) of section 147. Therefore he could not have issued a notice under section 149. [448 D] (ii) The report submitted by the Income tax officer to the Commissioner and the order of the Commissioner was produced. The order sheet recorded the reasons of the Income Tax officer as required by section 148. The report did not mention any reason for coming to the conclusion that it was a fit case for issue of notice under s.148. [449 E] (iii) The appellant could not be issued a show cause notice under S. 148. Further, the report submitted to the Commis sioner showed that the persons were name lenders and the transactions were bogus. Therefore, the order passed by the Commissioner must have been vitiated on account of non compliance with section 151. [450 G] (iv) The order of assessment was not invalid because it did mention any reasons for coming into the conclusion.

The appellant, a firm carrying on business in the manufacture of textiles and other goods, was started in 1902 and its business was carried on by two independent partnerships. The partners constituted a new firm which had been reconstituted by an agreement dated December 6, 1918. The firm was dissolved by an order of the Ruler of the erstwhile State of Bombay under which it was reconstituted. The appellant filed a suit for the recovery of certain sums of money from the respondent firm on the ground that the business in question was carried out by a firm which was dissolved and its businesses were split up into two and carried on with effect from November 13, 1947, by two separate independent partnership deeds. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the appellant was not entitled to relief under section 25(4) of the Income tax Act, 1922. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that (1) the business of the firm was carried in a different name and was not a dissolution by one of its partners; (2) the partnership was not dissolved on April 1, 1939, but on May 30, 1939 and therefore the business could be said to have been carried on at the commencement of the Indian Income tax (Amendment) Act, 1939. HELD: (1)(a) The business in which the appellant had been subjected to tax under the Act of 1918 was not one of dissolution of the partnership but only a change in the constitution of the partners and therefore, it could not be said that there was succession by another person for the purpose of section 26 or for the purposes of section 25 (4). [287 D] (b) The fact that he was not taken on in the original business also shows that the original firm had been dissolved. Therefore, the business continued in the hands of the same person who had paid tax under a statute of 1918 and the continuance of the person who was carrying on the business as a whole could not make him liable to tax for the period between April 1 1939 and March 28, 1939 when he was succeeded in his business by another firm. [287 G H] (c) The appellant was entitled to the benefit of section25(4). But it must be remembered that under section 26(2), a mere change in constitution does not count and sections 25(3) and 26(4)(a), do not apply at the same time. The business of a firm is carried on in a distinct new firm for the application of sub section (4) to a person who has paid tax thereunder for purposes of the Act. [286 G H; 287 A B] Jesingbhai Ujamshi vs Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay Moffusil, , referred to.

The respondent, who was the owner of a house in Bombay, filed a suit for partition and separate possession of a 7/24th share in two houses. The appellant 's case was that the suit properties belonged to the joint family consisting of her husband and his two sons. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the properties belonged exclusively to the respondent and that there was no prior partition and that the plaintiff was entitled to a 7 /24th undivided share. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decree of the trial court and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the suit property belonged to joint family; (2) the respondent had effected partition of the suit house between himself and his brothers; (3) the appellant 'S 's 1/24 share in the joint Hindu Family properties was only 1/25th, that the respondent 's father had effected a partition of that house by metes and bounds during her husband 's life time and the share which she would get in her husband"s interest upon his death; (4) the plaintiff 's share in her own property was only one half and that therefore, by reason of the provisions of section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, the pre conditions of section six were satisfied. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1(a) The suit properties belong to joint Hindu family and are self acquisitions. [766D] (b) The respondent 'S had effected the partition of his coparcenary property by metes & bounds during his life time between him and his sons. [764B C] (c) The appellant had a share in a joint family property, the fourth being, Khandappa 's wife 's husband '. The proviso to section 6 states that the decision of the appeal must turn on the meaning to be given to Explanation 1 of section6. [774C D] (d) The proviso does not provide further that in the circumstances of a case where there is no partition between the plaintiff and his son, the property should be deemed to have been allotted to him if a partition was effected between her husband & his two brothers. [754D E] (e) The Explanation to section six states that "the proviso shall not apply to a partition in respect of the joint Family property". The Explanation does not say that the share of the heirs must be ascertained on the basis that they bad separated from one another and had received a share therein during the life time of the deceased. [754F G] (f) The expression "the widow ' shall be deemed not to have received in the notional partition. The Explanation applies only to cases where there are two or more persons, who are relatives specified in class I of the Schedule to the Act and not as a limited owner. [758G H] (g) The explanation does not mean that the heirs should receive the property equal to that of a son. The expression 'the widow shall be "to have failed to furnish a return of his income". The proviso is intended to be explanatory of the provision for determining the share in property itself. It has to be read as the whole and the very first step, to ascertain the share, which the deceased had in the coparcenary property because after all, the plaintiff has a 1/4th interest in that share. [759A B] (2)(a) In the instant case, the respondent was not entitled to demand partition yet, if a partial partition took place between the appellant and his brother, the respondents would be entitled to receive a share equal to the appellant or her share in their interest. [761B C]. (b). The High Court was right in holding that section 6 did not provide for a rerograde step to determine the share. while section 6 does not prescribe any further procedure. [763C D].

The appellant Corporation, a public sector undertaking, was constituted under the Life Insurance Corporation of India Act, 1956. The Life Insurance (Emergency Provisions) Ordinance, 1960, came to be promulgated by the Central Government on January 19, 1956, providing for the vesting of the management of the life insurance business in the State of Kerala. Section 11(2) of the said ordinance provided that every whole time employee of an insurer whose controlled business had been transferred to and vested in it shall retire on completion of 58 years of age or at any time thereafter if his efficiency was found to have been impaired. The appellant Corporation was required to retire on completing 58 years from the date of retirement on or after 1st September, 1956 but before that date the Corporation decided to nationalise the life of its employees. In exercise of the power conferred by section 11(1) of Act, the management took over the management and appointed the appellant as an employee of the Corporation on or about May 31, 1956 and provided for its management. The respondent Corporation was directed to retire the appellant on completion Of 58 years. The Corporation thereupon decided to take over the appellant 's service till June 30, 1963 on giving him three months notice or salary in lieu thereof. In the meantime, the appellant had been compulsorily retired by the Corporation under section 11 of the Act. The High Court held that the employees belonging to Class I and Class II were entitled to continue in service till they attained the age of 60 years. Allowing the appeal by special leave, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1 The retirement age of employees of the respondent Corporation is a valid classification and Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution have not been violated.

The appellants wrote a letter to the President of India stating that the Judge had been given an impression that he was not a Judge but a politician who had come to Barwani in a closed cover addressed to the Chief Justice of Punjab and Haryana High Court. The letter stated that the Judges of the Bar Association were very poor and that they had failed miserably in all fields. The appellants took a copy of their letter to this Chief Minister, who was present at the hearing. They also wrote a note stating that if in view of this Hon 'ble Court the action of the deponent in addressing the letter in question constituted for any reason contempt of court, no one would be more sorry than the deponent himself. The High Court did not take any action against two persons on the letter written by them and dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the letter did not bear out any foundation for an action for criminal contempt. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The letter in the instant case was addressed by the deponent to the Governor of Punjab with copies to others with the sole object of conveying the opinion that the public expression by the Hon ' blemis sion of a Judge or this Court should steer clear of all avoidable controversial matters. [245E] 1.2 In order to prevent unwanted disclosure of its contents, the communication in question was brought personally by two members of the bar association, Bhiwani to Chandigarh in a open cover addressed by one of the members of Bar Association, Bhiwni to Chandigarh. The deponent further stated that there was no intention whatsoever on his part to scandalise the Honble Judge or the Court in any manner to weaken people 's faith in the administration of justice. [246G H] 1:3. The contents of the letter were not disputed and challenged. It was intended to be a privileged communication made solely with a view to uphold the dignity of the Court. In order that the action may be taken for any reasons contempt of Court, one would he more swer than the affidavit himself. Therefore, the deponent tender his apology to this Hon`ble Court for the same and prayed for its acceptance. [243A B] 1 :4. The matter did not constitute any contempt. The contempt proceedings were dropped.

The appellant, a company registered under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was carrying on business in the manufacture of textile and other articles. The company had made secret profits which it had not disclosed and had thus evaded payment of tax. The Income tax Officer, after investigation, found that the appellant had committed an offence under section 5(1) of the Act, and issued a notice to the appellant under section 6(5) Of the Act asking him to furnish certain material as detailed in Annexure 'B ' to the report of the Commission. On appeal by the appellant, the Appellate Tribunal held that the provisions of sections 5(2), 5(4), 6, 7 and 8 of the Indian Income tax Act were not applicable to the case and that section 5 (1) Of section 5 Of the said Act was ultra vires the Central Government. The High Court, on a reference under article 226, held that section 6 of the said Indian Income Tax Act did not apply to the present case as it had been made in accordance with the provisions contained in section 34 of the , and that the procedure prescribed by the impugned Act was a good substitute for that prescribed by section 7 Of the Indian Incometax Act. Held, that the proceedings taken under section 3(4) Of Act XXXVII of 1947 were not covered by section 5 of the Central Act. The procedure prescribed under the Act in so far as affects the persons proceeded against under that sub section being a piece of discriminatory legislation offends against the provisions Of article 14 of the Constitution and is thus void and unenforceable.

The appellant, a company registered under the Companies Act, 1913, was carrying on business as a commercial establishment. The primary objects of the Federation were to promote Indian business in matters of inland and foreign trade, transport, industry and manufacture, finance and all other economic subjects and to encourage or facilitate the export of goods, industrial undertakings and manufacturers. The appellant, an association of companies, was registered under section 26 of the , with its registered office at New Delhi. The Federation had a branch office in New Delhi and New Delhi etc. The establishment was not a commercial establishments within the meaning of section 2(5) of the Act. The Association was registered as a Commercial Establishment under section 2 (9) of that Act. In the year 1963, the appellant company filed an application for prosecution of its Secretary, the Federation, under the . The Chief Inspector of Shops and Establishments, Delhi, called upon the Federation to register its establishment and submit its report. On receipt of the report, the Registrar of Shops & Establishments, New Delhi, issued a notice to the Federation calling upon it to register the establishment 'and submit its objections. The Union filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order dated February 4, 1964 passed by the Chief Inspector. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the activity of the appellant was a " commercial establishment" within the definition of "commercial establishment". In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the activities of the Association were not a "business or trade" within section 2, (5) the application of the provisions of the . was not maintainable; and (ii) even if the activity was a ' commercial establishment ', the words "any business, business or profession" given in the Act would not take it out of the definition. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The activities of a registered society, charitable or other trust will not take the place of commercial establishment, and no part thereof could be paid as dividend or otherwise to any member. [354D] 2. (i). The High court was right in holding that since the Association was a company, it was an activity within the purview of section2(5), and the question whether the activity amounted to carrying on a business or trade was directly covered by the definition in section 2. [355E F] (ii). The definition of commercial Establishment includes "a 'shop ' and "commercial establishments" given therein. In view of the decision of this Court in R. K. Mittal 's case, the commercial or industrial entertainments were not taken away or distributed among its members. But that does not alter the 'fact that its activity is a trading or business activity. For all the foregoing reasons particularly in view of section 3(4) of Act, the High court would hold that the commercial and industrial entertainment was an element common to the definitions of " commercial establishments" and "industry". [355F G] (iii). The mere fact that the rendering or services is not specifically mentioned as an element of the term of " Commercial Establishment" does not necessarily mean something by which a profit is made. But putting aside the question, whether they carry on a trade or business in the premises in question, would lead to the conclusion that the activities were connected with trade and business generally. That was why the High Courts held that the business of the club was not "a commercial establishment", but a "commercial Establishment" within its meaning. [356G H] (iv). The word "business" is used in the context of section '2(4), for the purpose of finding out whether it carries on a commercial or trade, and not to be confined to a business. Secondly, it should be premises where (a) trade, business, or profession is carried on, or (b) any work in connection with or incidental or ancillary thereto is carried out. [337B C] (v).
