The assessee was a Hindu undivided family consisting of himself and his successors. The income tax authorities assessed the assessee to agricultural income tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, on the ground that the amount received by him as an allowance during the previous year of assessment was revenue income liable to tax under section 4(3)(viii) of the Act. The Appellate Tribunal held that from the language of the letter dated July 7, 1837 it was manifest that the right which was conferred was a right to a share of one fourth in the net land revenue collections after deducting costs of Tahsil establishment. On appeal by the assessee, the High Court held that the income tax was not agricultural income as defined in section 2(1)(a) of Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the allowance in question was revenue receipt and not taxable; and (ii) the source of the income was clearly the arrangement arrived at in 1837 and therefore it was not agriculture income as contemplated by section 2 (1)(b). HELD: The High Court was right in holding that the allowance was revenue. [707 D] The word 'derived ' is not a term of art but a term which is used in the definition itself. In the present case, the source and character of the assessee are altered when a part of the Income tax is appropriated by the appellant as his remuneration. Both the source as well as the character of income appropriated as remuneration due is again not the same as the nature of the receipt, a substantial part whereof is derived from lands used for agricultural purposes. [077 D] Commissioner of Inland Revenue vs Wesleyan and General Assurance Society, , referred to.

The respondents in C.A. No. 441 of 1981 were appointed as Supervisors Grade A on various dates in pursuance of a circular dated 6th November, 1962 issued by the Ministry of Defence, which provided that the Diploma holders who had been appointed as Supervisor 'A ' and in equivalent grades should be treated as having been promoted to Chargeman II. The appellants in CAs Nos. 441 and 442 of 1981 filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the said circular dated 4th April, 1983 and the judgment of this Court dated 2nd February, 1981. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the direction given by this Court on 2nd Febru ary, 1981 was not applicable to the case of the appellants as they had been promoted in pursuance thereof and that the respondents were entitled to be treated at par with the other similarly situated persons. In the appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants that the said Circular dated 6 th November,1962 was not a direct recruit ment Grade 'A but only such a Supervisor Grade 'B ' who immediately before the coming into force of the order dated 28th December, 1965 and the circular dated 20th January, 1966 stood in a class separate from those whose promotion were to be made thereafter. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The respondents in Civil Appeal No. 442 of1981 are on the same footing as they have been promoted before that date. [106G] 2. It is not a fit case for initiating any proceedings for contempt again st the respondents. [107A B] 3. It was not open to the appellants in Civil Appeals No.441 of 1981 to be granted the same benefits which were given by the Madhya Pradesh High Court to such of the petitioners before that Court w ho were Supervisors 'A" and were granted promotion as Chargeman I by its judgment dated 4 th April,1983. [108B] 4. It would not be a fit cases for initiating proceedings for Contempt again stan ding any proceedings thereafter. [109C D] 5. The contention of the respondents that these employees who had joined much later than 20th Januar y, 1966 could not be promoted to the post soon after the completion of 2 years ' service as Supervisor Grade A was rejected by this court on 4th February, 1982. [110D E] 6. It may also be noticed that in Civil appeal No. 440 of 1981 there is no dispute that the appellants of this appeal have in pur poses of the matter of promotion to the next higher grade and the order of this court dated 2 nd February,1981 has been given a back date promotion to them. [111E] 7. The question whether the Supervisors ' A ' who had not been granted the difference of back wages and promotion to higher posts on the basis of their back date promo tion as Chargemen I in the case was a matter which could be considered for promotion only in accordance with the normal rules and not merely on completion of two yea rs satisfactory continuous service. [112F G] 8. The fact that some Supervisors 'B who had already been promoted prior to the coming In force of this order dated 2 2 1981 were promoted before the came into force would not make any difference in the matter as the appellants have not been given the difference. Therefore, the appellants cannot be granted relief on the ground of their seniority in the back date promotions.

The appellant State Transport Authority, by its order dated February 1, 1984 granted three out of eleven permits to the Karnataka State Tourism Development Corporation. The first respondent was a stage carriage operator and the second respondent was the permit holder. The second respondent had to be denied the grant of permits since he had not got a certificate of approval from the Central Government. The appellant State Road Transport Corporation filed writ petitions in the High Court challenging the grant. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that having regard to rule of preference envisaged by the proviso to section 63(7) of the , the preference contemplated by the second proviso was not violative of article 14 and had to he struck down. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant State that (i) the first respondent had an equal chance to get a permit even on inter state route or notified area; (ii) the fourth respondent had been denied the benefit of the second part of the proviso; and (iii) the third respondent had not been able to get the certificate of the approval from Central Government because of the rule of priority envisaged by section 63 (7). Dismissing the appeals, this Court. HELD: 1. The scheme of the Act in the matter of grant of permit for stage carriages and contract carriage permits is very obviously the promotion of tourism and the approval of the Central Govern ment would be given to those operators of tourist cars and travel agents who may be expected to serve that purpose. [1019C] Sher Singh vs Union of India, ; , followed. Sher Singh 's case, overruled. Sher singh 's decision in Sher Singh was not correct. The State Transport Appellate Tribunal and the High Courts have failed to consider the merits of the claims of the Karnataka Road Transport Corpora tion and the private operators who did not get a certificate from the central Government, because of its rule of precedence contained in proviso to Section 63(1) of . [1010F] Sher singh vs Union Of India, , followed and applied. Sher Singha Singh vs State of Punjab, ; and Sher Singh & Ors. vs Union Territory of Chandigarh, ; referred to.

The respondent purchased a business carried on by the appellant. The business was transferred to the respondent and the respondent paid some amounts towards sales tax. The Sales Tax authorities attempted to recover the arrears of tax from the respondent as the purchaser of the business. The respondent contended that the State Government had no authority under its rule making power under section 19(1) and 19(2)(c) of the Act to create a legal fiction by which the transferee of the, business was constituted as the dealer liable to pay sales tax in respect of the turnover of the transferor. The High Court held that Rule 21 A was ultra vires and the State Legislature had no power under its Rule making power to create the transferee. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that Rule 23A was beyond the rule making powers of the State Govt. under section19(1). HELD: (i) The word 'assessment ' in the scheme of sales tax and income tax legislation is a term of varying import. The word is used sometimes to mean the computation of income, sometimes the determination of the amount of tax payable, and sometimes the whole procedure laid down in the Income tax Act for imposing liability on the tax payer. As the Judicial Committee observed that Rule 22A was ultra rites of the rule, it was not open to the State to rely on the instrument inter vivos between the transferor and the transferee and to contend that there is a liability created inter se between the State Govern ment on the one hand and the transferor on the other. [665 E F] Badridas Daga vs C.I.T., Bihar, ; , referred to. (ii) Rule 21A was not ultra vires of the Rule making powers under section 9(1)(c). The High Courts were right in holding that Rule21 A is beyond the Rule make power of the state Government either under section 10 or section 19 (2)(C) of Act. [664 E F; 664 B] Badrinas Daga V C. I.T.

The appellant was appointed senior jailor, Surendranagar District Jail. On March 6, 1953, the respondent Accountant General of Prisons, Saurashtra, served a charge sheet on him under section 4(1) of the Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1960, alleging that while he was serving at Surendaranagar District, he had committed certain acts of mis appropriation of food stuffs meant for prisoners, maltreatment of prisoners and acceptance of illegal gratification from them. The respondent pleaded guilty and pleaded that the charge was not a liability arising out of a contract but was a liability in respect of an actionable wrong other than breach of contract. The trial court held that the failure on the part of the competent authority to provide the plaintiff with a copy of the report of enquiry held against him, amounted to denial of reasonable opportunity contemplated by article 311(2) of Constitution and dismissed the suit. On appeal, the High Court held that there had been breach of article 311 (2) Of the Constitution as the respondent was not supplied with a notice under section 80 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, but pleaded that he had not asked for copy of his report and had not been prejudiced by non supply of the copy of such report. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court erred in holding that there was breach of Article 311(1). HELD: (i) The respondent was entitled under article 311 of the Constitution to compensation from the shipowners not only in respect Of his wages but also of the retainer which must be taken into account as earnings under a concurrent contract of service. [923 B] (ii) The High Court erred in ordering payment of arrears of salary to the appellant from the date of the suit till the date when the respondent filed his written statement and pleaded guilty. [936 C D] State of Bihar vs Abdul Majid, ; , referred to. (iii) The finding that the appellant was not supplying copy of a report of the enquiry held by the Enquiry Officer amounted to denying reasonable opportunity under article 31(2). The High court was therefore right in holding on the facts that there has been breach Of article 311. [981 C D].

The appellants were the owners of a coal mine. The respondents filed a suit for possession of the said land on the allegation that the appellant had encroached upon it and had rendered the remaining coal liable to be removed under the previous lease in favour of the appellants. The trial court held that the respondent had encroached on the land and passed an order for the value thereof by way of damages. On appeal, the High Court accepted the finding of the Subordinate Judge and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Courts in India had wrongly decided the question whether the respondents had knowledge of the trespass only within three years of the suit and not within three year in the circumstances of the case, and that the finding was vitiated by an error of law by the burden of proof having been wrongly thrown on the appellant. HELD: (i) The High Court was right in holding that the onus of proving the knowledge of his father wag on the respondents to prove that he had knowledge about the encroachment only within 3 years of his coming into possession and that it was not permissible for a court to reconstruct the plan with reference to revenue records when the plan is self contained and drawn to scale. [501 D] (ii) The onus of proof in the former sense is on the party who comes to Court to get a decision on the existence of certain facts which he asserts. In the present case, the burden was upon the appellant to prove the fact that the knowledge was within three yea years of its purchase and not beyond three years. [500 E] (iii) The burden of proving that the information given by the respondents was false lies on the plaintiff who asserts a right and it may be having regard to the circumstances, of each case, that the facts proved were not in his knowledge or belief. [50 F G] Talyarkhan vs Gangadas, Pat. 75 I.A. 206, referred to. (iv) The presumption under section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act is a rebuttable one and the onus is upon the plaintiff in these suits to prove affirmatively that he has the knowledge or knowledge of it. [51 F G]. Talykshan vs Gimmajanta, Pat, 75 I A.C.

The appellant was a crosscutter. The question for determination in this appeal was whether the order of discharge passed under r. 18(a) of the Standing Orders without holding any departmental inquiry was justified or not. Held, that the employer could defend the action under r., 18 (a) by leading evidence before the tribunal to show that there was in fact misconduct and therefore the action taken under r, 18 (b) was bona fide and was not colourable exercise of the power conferred on it under that rule. The appellant had failed to satisfy the Tribunal when it came to the conclusion that the exercise of power was bona fides and was mala fide. The Tribunal had rightly held that the order terminating the services of the appellant was bona bonafide and was therefore invalid. The Chartered Bank, Bombay vs The Chartered bank Employees ' Union, ; , referred to. Held further, that in a case where the termination of service is capricious, arbitrary or unnecessarily harsh on the part of the employer judged by normal standards of a reasonable man that may be cogent evidence of victimisation or unfair labour practice, it would have jurisdiction to intervene and set aside such termination. The fact that the misconduct was proved did not justify an inference that there had been in fact mis conduct. The Industrial Tribunal had no power to inquire into the causes that might have led to termination of the service under r 18 (c). The appellant could not rest its case merely on r.18 (a), and it could not be said that the tribunal had gone wrong in holding that the action was bona bona fide.

The appellant was the receiver of a theatre belonging to the respondent. The receivers granted a lease of the theatre on certain terms and conditions. The appellant filed a suit for declaration that as sub lessee or licensee under law it was entitled to obtain and remain in possession of the cinema, and that the respondents were estopped from denying its rights to exhibit motion pictures in the theatre. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the appeal in limine. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The question whether a party is entitled to lead evidence or to put questions in cross examination of the plaintiff 's witnesses cannot form the subject matter of an issue. [445 B] (ii) The expression "case" is not limited in its import to the entirety of the matter in dispute in an action. This Court has recorded a finding that the agreement dated December 1, 1960 created a lease and that it was not even averred that it had been a lease. The High Court proceeded to decide matters on which no decision was till then recorded by the Trial Court and which could not be decided by the High court until the parties had opportunity to lead oral evidence thereon. [441 G H] (iii) The High court has recorded findings that the appellant was entitled under section 28 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 to obtain an order for exhibiting exhibit motion picture in the cinema theatre under the agreement. [442 C D] (iv) The trial Court had not decided any issues at all. It had also held that the question asked in cross examined by the appellant did not decide any issue at that stage. The Trial Judge was therefore right in holding that the questions asked were already concluded by the consent decree in suit No. 149 of 1960. [443 D E] (v) The order passed by the trial Court is set aside and the Trial court is directed to dispose of the suit.

The respondent was appointed as a pilot Officer in the Indian Air Force and was confirmed on 30.8.1979. The appellant, who was an officer of the Indian Army, was granted permanent commission in the I.A.F.I. for a period of one year w.e.f. 1st March, 1983. On 20th August, 1979 he was declared unfit by a medical board and was re instated from I.P.S. to the post in question on 30th August 1985. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging his order of termination which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the order of appointment could not be sustained and the Writ Petition was liable to be allowed. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The order of the High court dated 24th March, 1988 directing that the respondent was entitled to salary upto 30th of August 1985 if the order was found to be an invalid one. It is on this basis that the High Courts while setting aside the order by its order dated 24.3.1988 directed that the respond ent was entitled for salary upto the period he was entitled. The High Court had, therefore, while setting it aside the said order of dismissal, directed that respondent be reinstated in service with full back wages and allowances due to him till 30th September, 1985 if he did not do so. [243D E] 1.2. The fact that no order of extension had been sanctioned by the Governor beyond 30th8, 1985, was not a ground for interference by this Court under Article 136 of the Constitution. [244E F] 1:3. The view taken by the High COurt is wholly unsustainable. [245F G] 2.1 The respondent was employed only under a contract which specified the term of his appointment which extended only upto 30.08.1985. Since it is admitted that no orders of extension have been sanctioned, the respondent could not claim to be reinstated. [246G H] 2:2. In the instant case, the HighCourt had while setting the order dated 26th July 1988 directed that he was enti tled to salary till 30.9.1985 if the Order of termination of service served on him on 29.3, 1985 was found not to be illegal or unjustified. [247A] 2 :3. In view of the specific direction given by the Court in its order, the State Government had directed that it would be made available forthwith to the petitioner by way of an appointment. The petitioner had not urged before the Court that the Order dated 26.7.1988 extending his period of service till 30st August, 1985 had been liable to he ignored and that he should be treated as a person regularly appointed in Government service entitled to continue till he attained 58 years of age.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the evidence of the eye witnesses was not sufficient to convict him as there was no motive for the murder and his version was more probable than the version of the prosecution. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The discrepancies in the evidence were of a minor character and that they had been unduly magnified by the Sessions Judge. [368E] 2. It is obvious that the High Court was justified in interfering with the order of acquittal merely because another view is also possible. The principles are now well settled. At one time it was thougly thou ht that an order of conviction could be set aside for "substantial and compelling reasons" only and Courts used to launch on a search to discover those "substantial or compelling reasons". However, the circumstances were such as would show that the witnesses had been subjected to cross examination which was not suggested by the prosecution that the accused made a gesture as if he was stabbing the deceased. The evidence of P. Ws. 1 to 3 and the evidence given by them was corroborated by the evidence on record. [369F G] 3. In some cases Ramabhupala Reddy & Ors. vs State of Rajasthan, ; , Bhim Singh Rup Singh vs State Of Rajasthan, A.I.R. 1971 S.C. 460; Bhim Singh, Rup Singh & Ors., vs State, of Rajasthan; , and Khem Karan & Ors vs State (Delhi Administration) ; , applied. 4. The fact that the victim could have received the injury if she was standing, it did not follow that the injury could have been received in the circumstances mentioned by the accused. [370A B] 5. In the instant case, the High court was justified on airy and fanciful doubts. It was not justified in rejecting the evidence. The appeal is dismissed.

The appellant, a Judge of the Supreme Court, was appointed as a Judge in the High Court of Madras. He was given the power to appoint Judges of the High Courts and the High court by warrant under his hand and seal after consultation with the Chief Justice of India. The President of India, however, issued an order dated September 27, 1979 appointing a Judge for the purpose of removal of a Judge from his office. The appellant challenged the validity of the said order on the ground that it was violative of article 14 of the Constitution as he was not given the first opportunity to be heard before the order of removal was passed. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the President had no power to remove a Judge either of the Judges or of the Chief justice of a High Court and that the second opportunity to make an application for prosecution under section 6(1)(c) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 was not available to him. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the President has not been given the sole power or the exclusive power to grant sanction for prosecution of a judge of the Delhi High Court; (ii) the provisions of section 6 (1)(C) of Act 1 of 1947 are applicable only to a Judge who is employed in connection with the affairs of the Union and is not removable from his duties under article 124(4); and (iii) the power of removal under section 7 of the Act is not available for prosecution for an offence punishable under section 5 of the . Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The provisions of clause (e) of sub section (1) of section 5 are applicable to a person who is appointed in connection With the affairs or administration of the State and cannot be prosecuted without sanction under section 4(2). [236D] 2. The word "court" in clause (c) has to be given its widest connotation so as to include judges of the highest status, even though they are not removable by the wide definition of the expression in the Act but whose category for the grant of sanction is not envisaged by section 6 of the Criminal Procedure Code. [236E] 3. The words "courts" and "other authorities" used in clause(e) have to be read as a part of the scheme under which the public servant is required to furnish particulars of his assets with reference to which the disproportion and his inability to satisfactorily account can be inferred. In the case of Judges of High Courts, and Judges of other High Courts the provisions contained in clauses (4) and (5) of Article 124 have to he given some meaning which would place the burden on the prosecution, howsoever light, to make out a prima facie case for obtaining sanction of the competent authority under section6. [237E F] 4. The expression "court ' has been defined in clause 2(a) to mean a court having jurisdiction over any matter pending before it and includes a Judge or a Judge not removable therefrom by or with the sanction of Central Government. The term "court " is used in cl. (e), which means an appellate Court, and includes the HighCourt. [238F] 5. The power to punish a judge under section 3(1) is conferred on the President of the States and the Supreme Courts are invested with the same powers as are vested in the Central Government by the Constitution. The conferment of such power is not contemplated by section 2(c). It is for this reason that the word "Court" has to mean the Court competent to appoint and it is in this manner that Section 6( 1)(c), is attracted. [239H; 240A] 6. The constitutional functionaries, therefore, have no legal sanction behind it making it justiciable. [240B] 7. The Constitution, while providing for the procedure for prosecution, has not conferred any power on the Court to remove or dismiss a Judge.

The appellant was a member of the Sahas ' community. Abhoy Pada Saha and Sudhir Kumar Mondal were born in the said constituency. The contestants at the election held on various grounds including the Saha 's caste, subcastes, etc., claimed to be a member thereof as a member. The Tribunal rejected this claim holding that the appellant belonged to the "Kolri" community which was a Scheduled Caste and not a member belonging to the Schedule Caste specified in item 40 of the Presidential List of 1950. The High Court held that the said entry was not a sub caste within the Sunri caste group within the meaning of section 2(a) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. In appeal by special leave, HELD : (i) The Tribunal had gone wrong in considering the Saha s 's claim to be an independent caste. [391 C] (ii) The finding that Sahas were a wholly independent caste was altogether irrelevant to the point in issue. Evidence could alter the natural interpretation of the words in the Order. For the same reason, the correct interpretation of item 40 was that it indicates men of the Sunari District and those parts of the Purnea District which had been transferred to West Bengal were not to be considered as belonging to a Scheduled caste. That would show that where the exclusion is by a test other than a caste group, the Order expressly says so. It is natural to think that if the excluded Sahas are those Sunri sity members within the same kind, they would have said so; it would then have read " Sunri excluding those who bore the surname Saha". [391 G H] (iii) The High Courts were in error in interpreting the item on the evidence in the case as they appear to have done.

The appellant was the tenant of a flat on the second floor of a building in which he had a share. The landlord filed a complaint against the appellant under section 18(1) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, for receiving a sum of Rs. 30,000 as consideration for putting the complainant in vacant possession of the flat and an additional amount of Rs 2,000 for the furniture and the deposit of Rs 27,500 as consideration. The Magistrate convicted him under section 19(2) of that Act and sentenced him to pay a fine of Rs 30,0001. On appeal by the appellant the High Court acquitted him but on appeal by special leave it was contended that the offence arose only when the complainant paid the sum of money in respect of the furniture, and that the Magistrate had no jurisdiction to try the case. Held, that the words "the relinquishment of his tenancy of any premises" in section 19 (1) (c) of Bombay Rents. Hotel and lodging House Rates control Act, LVII of 1947, were not used in the Transfer of Property Act but only meant for the transfer by a tenant of his interest which was made unlawful under section 15 of that act. The words " the relinquishment of tenancy of an tenancy ofany premises" occurring in section 108(1)(c) did not occur in the transfer of the tenancy and therefore the offence under section 16 of the Act arose only on receipt of any sum or consideration as a condition of the lease.

The appellant company was a partnership firm. It had its factory at the time of the agreement with the appellant and as their demands were not accepted, the Government made a reference to the Industrial Tribunal under section 10(1) (d), Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, for adjudication. The Tribunal took note of the various factors which were required to be taken into consideration in arriving at its conclusion that the company was in an extremely high scale and it would not be possible for the appellant to bear the additional financial burden. It also observed that the dearness allowance would be available only on a slab system, and that it would be difficult for the company to bear such a situation. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the award of the Industrial Disputes (Bombay) Tribunal, Maharashtra, contending that the existing wage scales were fair and reasonable and in any event in ranging the retrospectivity back to 1st January, 1976, when the new scheme was introduced by the Government, the dearness allowances would be payable at 10% of the basic wage subject to a minimum of Rs. 150/ per month. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the new schemes were fair, and reasonable on the basis of the increase in the basic pay scales. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that having regard to the financial capacity of the company, the Tribunal erred in making the wage scales retrospective and in making its award retrospective and, therefore, the change in the dearness structure was not called for from the company and the same was submitted (i) by the Tribunal; (ii) by reason of the introduction of the new pay scale, the new scales were being introduced in the pay scales retrospective from 1st February, 1976; (iii) by virtue of the amendment made by the Industrial Dispute Act, the existing scheme of dearness allowance and house rent allowance was to be treated as a feature of the wage structure; and (iv) by an amendment of the award dated December 20, 1978, the original award had been made on the same day. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The new scheme introduced by Government for revising the existing structure with flat increases in each category was patently clear from a comparison of the existing pay scales and the revised pay scales pertaining to different categories. [179F] 2.1 The Tribunal had given satisfactory reasons for adopting a different mode and it did not reveal that there was any opposition by the company or the Union made an application under Rule 31 of the industrial Disputes ( Bombay) Rules, 1957 seeking a correction of an error apparent on the face of the record. [180G] 2(a) The Tribunal was wrong in holding that revision of wage scales was retrospective and it had no power to revise the existing schemes by which dearness allowance was being granted. [181B C] 2.(b) The amendment made in the award by the State Government on December 20. 1978, by which the new scale would yield but a very small and almost a token increase in dearness allowance, did not amount to an alteration of the pay structure. [182C D] 2 (c) The additional financial liability was considered to be Rs. 100/ and the Tribunal had taken into account the rise in the rise of the dearness pay scales in the category of Draftsmen and Rs. 50/ in the case of other categories. Since there was no opposition by it, the award was made on December 22, 1978. [183E F] 2:2. The additional dearness liability was not considered to have been proved by the Union that it was cognizant of the intention of the Tribunal to provide a flat increase to the pay of each workman in addition to the benefits conferred by the revised scale and other awarded reliefs. [184G] 3.1 In view of the fact that there had been to increase the dearness Allowance, the additional dearness allowance could not always be said to have resulted in serious anomalous situations.

The respondent, an award made by the Industrial Tribunal fixing the pay of the employees at Rs. 2/ per day and in pursuance thereof, the management of the appellant had entered into an agreement with the respondents that effect would be given to the wage structure prescribed by the award. The appellant contended before the High Court that section 15 of the Act was inapplicable because the wages prescribed by it were not payable under any award or settlement between the parties or order of a court, and that the claim of the respondents was barred by limitation. Held, that the provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, are applicable to the case as the wages fixed by the Award did amount to wages as defined by section 2(vi) of the , and it also argued that the wages payable under an award could not be included in the definition of wages prescribed under section 2 (vi). The provisions of section 2 of the Bombay Act were applicable only to the wages which were fixed by an award. Section 2(iv) as it stood at the relevant time provided, inter alia, that any remuneration payable under a award or settle ment between the employer and his employees shall be included therein in the main definition in section 2.(vi). In view of the definition contained in section 3(vi), the provisions made by an Industrial Tribunal for determining the wages of the workmen for instance, need not be express and can be implied; but they must be terms which arise out of the contract of employment. The development of industrial law during the last decade bears testimony to the fact that on references made under section 10(1) of Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1958, the said awards supplant contractual terms in respect of matters covered by them and are substituted for them.

The appellant was a Sub Assistant Surgeon in the Public Works Department, Pepsu. He was entrusted with the work of obtaining signatures or thumb impressions of the employees before wages were paid to them. The sanction under section 197(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure was necessary for prosecuting the appellant under section 409 and the Chief Secretary, Home Department sent a communication to the appellant that he had been "directed to convey sanction of the Government to his prosecution". The Chief Secretary sent a reply to the letter. The Chief Secretaries sent a telegram to the effect that he did not receive the amount in question and that by this expedient he received Rs. 51 as gratification from the employees employed in the works, and that he misappropriated the same. The appellant contended that the prosecution was bad for want of sanction under s. 197(l) of Code of criminal Procedure. Held, that the sanction under sec. 197 (1) was necessary before the appellant could be prosecuted under section409, and the absence of such sanc tion was fatal to the maintainability of the prosecution. The fact that the entrustment and/or dominion were in an official capacity, and it is equally evident from the evidence that the appellant received the sum of Rs.51 alleged to have been misappropriated as Sub division Officer and he admits receipt of the same, a thumb impression as against his name. The presumption under section 196(l)(a) of Cr. P.C., could not be drawn up against the appellant in view of the fact that he was not present at the time when the offence was committed while he was actually engaged in the performance of official duties.

The appellant was a banking company incorporated in the State of Cochin with branches in that State. The income tax authorities determined its assessable income under the Travancore Income tax Act, 1922, but did not include the loss from the branch situate outside the State. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the business of the assessee being one and indivisible for the purpose of determining the amount assessable to income tax it was entitled to deduct the losses incurred in British India and in States other than Travancore State, and (ii) the proviso to section 24(1) of the Indian Income tax (Amendment) Act, 1941, which provided that where a loss sustained is a loss of profits or gains which would but for the proviso would be in excess of the provisions of section 4(3), the assessee was entitled under the amended section to deduct such losses from his income. HELD : The proviso to s 24(i) of Indian Income Tax Act, as it stood before its amendment, provided that "the total world income" of an assessee includes income, profits and gains accruing within or without British India. Therefore, to say that business in section 10 means business in British Indian or business the profits or gain of which are taxable in India is to ignore the definitions and sections 3, 4 and 6 of the Act. [262 D E] The proviso must be read with section 14(2)(e) and it was not a modification of the substantive enactment by providing an exception and taking out as it were from the main enactment, a portion which, though not an Indian State, was expanded into " income", profits and losses "in any other Indian State or in the case of Travancore State" so divide business. But then it was said that the words "a loss of profit or gains " occurring in section 2(15) of Act 1 of 1941 should be read as " a loss " in the latter part of the proviso, and that the word "income " in section 4 (3) meant income " which in the former case was expanded to include income profits and gain accruing within British India, and therefore it necessarily applied to the head " business " in that head. [263 E F] The words " income " occurring therein were not there in the section but only a provision which would cover an exception. The use of these words does not circumscribe the proviso. Section 24(2) of that Act was intended to give effect to the main provisions of the main section i.e. section 24 (1) which was amended by the Indian Finance Act, 1942. [264 G H] The object of the Income tax law is to tax " income ", a term which it does not define. It is expanded no doubt into " total world" but it is used in the sense of an addendum or dealing with a subject which is foreign to the principal enactment. The word " income" is used as meaning "income". [265 B C] The Commissioner of Income tax vs Shaw Wallace and Co., (1936) L.R. , referred to.

The appellant company was incorporated in January 1946 as a Private Limited Company. The respondent company was converted into a Public Limited Company and the Head Office of the Company was at Calcutta. In July 1947, the Company took over the business of the partnership firm of the Shaw Wallace & Co., which had been doing business in India for about 60 years. On the question whether it should be fixed at 58 or at 60, HELD : (i) The Tribunal has rightly held that the age of retirement should be 58 and not 60. [426 B] (ii)The Tribunal was right in holding that the date of retirement of the appellant workmen should be the 58 or 60 years in view of the fact that the company had been successful in their claim for fixing the age at 60 years, and that the Company may in its discretion and with the express or implied consent of the employee concerned continue an employee after he attains that age. [427 C] Dunzlop Rubber Co. Ltd., vs Workmen, ; , followed. (iii)The question whether the concern should be fix at 58 was a matter which was not raised before this Court in the present case. The Tribunal had taken considerable pains to perform this duty and it has ultimately persuaded itself to hold that no such trend is established in fact. [ 428 D] Dunnop Rubber Company Ltd., V. Workmen, , referred to. (iv)The award of the Tribunal was not challenged before this court. It was contended on behalf of the workmen that the trend in Bombay region had been to fix the retirement age at 58 years and that it had taken some more time in the region for doing so. The appellant company did not dispute that the figures given by the various concerns were correct.

The appellant company was incorporated in 1961 and its incorporation in the year 1961. In the year 1962, the company filed a petition under section 237(b) of the , for the issue of a writ prohibiting the Board from giving effect to the order dated May 19, 1965 passed by it. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the Board had acted on material extraneous to the matter and therefore the Board bad no power to make an order under section 235(b). In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The power conferred on the Central Government by section 237 is merely administrative but not judicial. [330 D] (2) The Board has power to constitute the company Law Board, to delegate its function to the Board and to control (a) the affairs of the company; (b) the persons concerned in the management of the affairs thereof were guilty of fraud, misfeasance and other misconduct towards the company and its members. [334 E] (3) The order dated April 4, 1965 was passed by the Chairman on behalf of the Board. It was not a mere administrative one but an executive order. [328 G] (4) The powers conferred on it under section 236(b), are discretionary. The power is conferred on a Tribunal to delegate the function of the Chairman to the board and to regulate its own procedure. The Board is invested with all such powers as are necessary for carrying out the purposes of the Act. [ 330 B C] (5) The Central Government has power under section 9(b)(1) to delegate it to the company, but it has not exercised that power in a manner which is contrary to the requirements of the statute. The appellants were convicted under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to 5 years rigorous imprisonment. The High Court confirmed their conviction but reduced the sentence to one year 's rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rs. 100/ . In appeal by special leave, HELD : (i) If there is other evidence to connect an accused with the crime itself, however small the finding of the stolen property with him is a piece of evidence which connects him further with the offence. There is then no question of presumption. The evidence corroborating the other evidence already against him was a piece Of evidence which connecting him with the dacoity and looted the property. [724 D E] (ii) If the gap of time is too large, the presumption that the accused was concerned with the murder itself may be drawn. It is not necessary to state categorically in this case that within the short time available, these goods could have been easily disposed of by receivers till such time as the original offenders could take them away. [700 E F] (iii) The fact that the goods stolen were a large quantity of cloth taken for sale to the market does not make any difference. It all depends upon the circumstances under which the discovery of the fruits of crime is made with a particular accused.

The petitioners, who were manufacturers of 'Tolinner ' within the meaning of Section 5 of the , sought to challenge the vires of section 5 of t he Act on the ground that the section gave an unguided, unchanalised and arbitrary power to the State Government to include any substance as poison for the purpose of restriction to be imposed on the posses sion for sale and sale of the same. The petitioners contended that since the Act was a Central enactment it was possible of unjust and unjustified discrimination between the two manufacturers and their products, and that the impugned notification was violative of article 14 of the Constitution. Dismissing the writ petition, HELD: 1.1 The provisions of neither Section 2 nor 5 nor the impugned Notification are hit by any consti tutional limitation. [223E] 1.2 The Act is intended to regulate the importation, possession and sale and the sale of a specified poison for purposes of committing murder or mischief by poisoning cattle appears to it to be of such frequent occurrence as to render restriction on the possessi tion thereof desirable. Any substance which is used for purposes mentioned therein can definitely be declared as poison. That is what the Government have done in this case. It has become a notorious fact, which is not disputed that the Act is an Act intended to control over the traffic in poisons. Some substances which the Govern ment consider its possession for sale or sale to be regulated in the interest of health and safety of the society. This limitation is inherent in the scheme of the Act itself. Of course no comprehensive definition can be given to the word poison. Under this term it nobody can be considered to have an absolute right to carry on any trade or business. [222G H; 223A B] 1:3. The provisions contained in neither Section 3 nor 5 or the impugned notifications are hit either by any of the provisions of law. [225B C] 2.1 It is a busi ness which can be termed even as inherently dangerous to health and fire safety of society in view of the rampant misuse and sale to the poor, weak and helpless as an intoxicant. A law in such circumstances can regulate the trade. This pos session may be a dangerous one which can he termed even though inherently dangerous. [226C D] 2:2 It is not necessary that the same substance should be declared an poison for tho entire country. The notification and its application to any area would depend on the necessity to declare the substance as poisoning on the particular facts and situation prevailing in that area and the need to regu lute the possession and sell in that areas. No question of discrimination can arise in such circum stances. [227D E] 2 :3 The provisions in neither section 2 nor5 nor the notification are hit, by any con tentional limitation, and the writ peti tion is accordingly dismissed.

The appellant firm was carrying on business in drugs, chemicals, mercury, camphor and silk yam and as money lenders. The assessee firm had dealings with the benefits of partnership, each with a firm known as M/s. Bhojaji Sobhachand, partners of which the appellant was the father of the firm. In the books of account of the appellants which were maintained by the Income tax Officer in the year of account ending on October 31, 1951, the amount due to the assessee was shown as a bad debt written off as irrecoverable in the books. The Income tax officer disallowed the claim holding that the debt did not arise in the course of money lending business and that the transaction was mere accommodations which could have no bearing to the regular business carried on by the assessee. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner agreed with the Income Tax Officer and held that the amount was a bad and doubtful debt in its money lending and therefore the assessee 's claim for deduction under section 10(2)(xi) of the Indian Income tax Act was not maintainable. The Tribunal however, allowed the appeal of the assessee holding that it had failed to establish that the loan did not exist which could be taken in the ordinary course of business of the appellant. On a reference made by the High Court under section 66(1) of Income Tax Act, the High court held that on the facts and in the circumstances of the case the Tribunal was right in holding that debt of Rs. 2,68,385/ written off by the appellant in his books of accounts as irrecoverable could have been no debt representing loss sustained in the other business. On the question whether the debt of the respondent was a ' bad and disputed debt ' within the meaning of section 10 (2) (xi) Of the Indian Incometax Act, 1922, HELD : The High Court has found that the monies sent by the assesses to the Bombay firm were not loans made in the normal course of its money lent business nor in respect of any other business of assessee. This finding covers the entire amount sought to be deducted. [419 D] (1) The question whether on the circumstances and in particular in favour of the asses see are debts due to him in the usual course of his business is not a catalogue of a loan advanced in the special course of the money lending, business or for any other purpose as preferred to para 7 above. [420 D] In the present case the amounts were not sent to the respondent as loans made by them in the regular course of their money lending. The fact that the assessee firm was the son of the partners of the Bombay firms does not make any difference because they are loanees who have a large share in the Bombay Firm.

The petitioners were the owners of certain lands which were acquired by the respondents under the provisions of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. The petitioners filed petitions in this Court challenging the acquisition on the ground that they had not made within two years of the notification making the declaration under section 4 of the Act. This Court granted interim stay of further proceedings in respect of the acquisition of the said lands. In these appeals by special leave, it was contended for the petitioners that as the awards in these cases have not been made within one year from September 20, 1984, the entire acquisition proceedings had lapsed and therefore, they were not entitled to be made within three years from the date of publication of the declaration. Dismissing the Special Leave Petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. The fact of the stay orders was highly material in the determination of these special leave petitions. [565E] 2. The facts of the case are highly material and there is no reference in the Special leave petitions to any to the stay order and it is beyond dispute that the fact of stay orders were highly material. [566F] 3. The question whether the awards were made within the stipulated time was a matter of direct bearing on the question raised and the non disclosure of the same certainly amounts to suppression of material facts. If he fails to do so, and suppresses material facts his application is liable to be dismissed. [567G H] 4. The High Court granted stay of the further proceedings. Whatever the ultimate effect of the order was highly important in the deter mination of these Special Leave petitions, it cannot be rejected on the grounds that the non production of the very same certainly amount to suppression. [568A B] 5. If the respondents fail to do any thing and suppress material facts, his application was liable to he dismissed. The special leave Petitions are accordingly dismissed.

The appellant bank claimed that under cl. (ii) of the Sastry award the adjustment basic pay in the new scale should be as on January 1, 1959 and not on January 31, 1959. The appellant contended that the words "subject to rules (i) to (iii) " in cl. 2(a) of para. 5(1) of its Sastry Award were wide enough to include in the definition of "on January 1. 1962" the expression subject to r. 4(a). Held, that the appellant bank 's case was not covered by cl. 3(a), (b) and (c) of Para. 5. The adjustment basic salary as on February 1, 1962 was Rs. 2,000 and the appellant was entitled to two increments under sub cls. (a) and(b). The appellant bank had been given a benefit of the new scales for that area and therefore the adjustment in the Sastry Award was not justified. Prakash Chand Mehra vs Chand Mehra, ; , followed. In the matter of adjustment, all efficiency bars, whether in the previously existing or in the scales provided by the Sastry Act, as modified by the Labour Appellate Tribunal 's award as modified or the maximum of that scale or the actual basic pay as on 1st January 1959, as the case may be, should be given over and above what has been worked out under sub cl. 5, are subject to cl. 4 (a). The fact that by oversight sub cl.(d) of el. (iv) was not made a separate clause would make no difference for sub cl (b), because the adjustment of the appellant 's basic pay had to be given after adjustments have been made under sub clauses (a),(b) or (c).

The appellants, who were owners of a plot of land in 1854, applied for the allotment of a five star hotel. The Director of the Zoo, after considering the objections filed by the appellants, recommended to the State Government that the land should be relinquished in favour of the appellants. The Minister for Urban Development submitted a note to the Chief Minister on June 29, 1981 stating that the Hastings House property may be offered to the I.T.D.C., and the Begumbari land may be given to the Taj Group of Hotels. The Lt. Governor forwarded his reply pointing out that the said proposal was not acceptable to the Zoological Department because the Hub Group of hotels had no access to the said plot of lands. The Col lege Minister also pointed out that there were already in existence a number of multistoreyed buildings all around the land proposed to be leased out to the T.D., and that the Taj group of Hotels who considered it necessary to negotiate with them in regard to the construction of a Five Star Hotel, had become public knowledge and newspapers. The matter was taken up by the Minister for Special Leave to appeal. On behalf of the State it was contended that the decision taken by the Cabinet on February 12, 1981 was merely to enter into negotiations with the ITDC and the Taj Groups were not willing to accept the land in question as they had been given to them. It was further submitted that the Lt. Col. Minister had no authority to grant the lease of the said land to the Indian Hotels. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The decision taken on February 13, 1981 is merely to be understood in the context of the Government 's policy and it is on a total evaluation of various considerations which have weighed with the Government in taking a particular action. [260F] 1.2 In view of the fact that the State had made available to the Court all the relevant documents so as to satisfy the court about the propriety of its action, the Court would not strike down governmental action as invalid on this ground unless it is clearly satisfied that the action was unreasonable or not in public interest. [262G H] 1:3 The principle of natural justice had not been observed and that it was not forgotten that if the land was to be allotted to the foreign hotel, the Government did not have the power to deal with the land.

The assessee, a Hindu undivided family, had a cash balance of Rs.4,299 in the books of M/s. Pearls & Beads. The assessee had a large cash balance with him and had also a sum of Rs,50,000 to his son. The Income Tax Officer, who was of the view that the said amount should be included in the net wealth of the assessee, issued notices under section 10(1) of the Act calling upon the assessee to debit his account to the extent of Rs 1,50 lakhs and credit the respective amounts in the names of the aforesaid persons. The respondent contended that there was no valid gift of Rs 25,000 by him to his sons and therefore the amount had been wrongly included in his net wealth by the Income Tax officer and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The Appellate Tribunal held that the assessee did not make a valid gift but only oral instructions were given to the assessee and that there were sufficient funds at the disposal of the donor by reason of which he could make the gift by such book entries. On appeal, the High Court held that there had been no valid gifts. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that there is no valid transfer of the principal amounts as there was a valid transfer and the interest paid in respect of the accounts standing in the name of the donees was allowable as a deduction in the hands of the asses see. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was in error in answering the question in the manner it did. [130D] 2.1 In order to decide whether the assessee had made a valid gifts or trust in respect thereof, the Income tax Officer must have regard to the facts and circumstances of each case other than those of the factum of gift, it could not be said that the donee had not retained the possession and enjoyment of the property to the entire exclusion of the donee or to the whole exclusion of his donor. [131E] 2:2 In the instant case, the assessee was the karta of a Hindu Undivided Family. On 20th November, 1956, the assesseee made a gift of certain amounts by way of gift in his favour and the gift was effected by debiting the assessee 's account in the firm and corresponding credits to the accounts of L and K. The sums were en tained in the account books of the Hindu undivided Family with the amount shown in the accounts regularly for some time, until a bank from which C had obtained an overdraft objected to such crediting of interest. On a reference made by the High court, the question was whether there was valid gift or trust. [132G H] 2(a) The assessee was not appearing when the money was transferred by debit ing the assessee. It was only oral instruction given to him to make a proper gift. The accounts were not maintained in the records of the company. The amounts were not available with the assessee for the amount in question on that date. [133B] (b) The High court was in agreement with the Tribunal and it held that section 10 did not apply to the gifts made by transfer in the assessee firm by debitings in the balance sheet. There was no evidence of acceptance of entries made in the book of account and by the declaration, nor any such entry was made in his books of account. [134C] (c) The Tribunal had correctly held that under section 123 of the , in case of gift of movable property, the transfer may be effected by delivery. In that view of the matter, except to the limited extent indicated above, the entries in the return books could not effectuate gifts.

The Orissa Superior Judicial Service Rules, 1963 were framed by the State Government under article 309 of the Constitution. Under Rule 3(1) of the said Rules the Governor is empowered to appoint a person as the Chief Justice of the High Court and to add or sub cadre to the cadre of district judges. The rules provided that the Chief justice shall be the sole authority to effect the necessary transfers. Rule 4(2) provides that the secretaries to the Government shall not in any way tamper with the existing posts. Rule 5(1)(b) provides for appointment of secretaries and legal remembrancer. Rule 6(1), (3) and (4) provide that the Secretary to the government shall not, in the exercise of his functions, continue in that post for an unduly long time. The High Court held that the power to appoint the secretors to the Gov ernment was exclusively vested in the Chief Judicial Magistrate who had no authority to make any appointment and that the Government had no power to fill up the posts by transfer of judicial officers. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Courts were not competent to issue a writ of mandamus against the government as well as the concerned officers to implement the orders in question. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The power to make rules under article 235 is conferred on the Chief judicial Magistrate who is subordinate to him and falls within the exclusive jurisdiction of the Governor and fall to be made by the High court as part of the control vested in it by article 235. [161F] 2. Under Article 235, the Governor has a right to ask the High Commissioner not to interfere with its functions. The control over the judiciary is that of the Chief Secretary. The executive cannot know the requirements of a particular Court. It is open to the High Commis sioner to fix the period during which he may hold any executive post. [162G H] 3. The Government has a power to issue directions in respect of the other officers under its control for filling up such executive posts as may require the services of judicial officer. The government, in its turn should appreciate the anxiety of the respondent State that judicial officers should not be allowed to acquire vested interest in the secretariat. [164A B] 4. The Chief Secretary to Government is competent to fix a period duringwhich he may held any executive posts. At the end of that period, the government is bound to allow him to go back to his parent department unless the High Cour tial Officer agrees to spare his services for some more time. [165G H; 166A] 5. The State Government has no power under article 233 to appoint an officer as a district and sessions judge. It cannot, as contended by the respondent, be said that he was placed at the disposal of the government for any definite period. [166B C] 6. The order of the Government posting Shri B.K. Patro as District and Sessions Judge is set aside.

The appellant, a co sharer in the State of Haryana, had filed a suit for pre emption against the respondent No. 1 and the co sharers of the vendors. The mother State, the State, had also filed an appeal against the decree passed by the trial court. The High Court dismissed the appeal holding that there was no infringement of Article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that if an outsider is introduced as a co co shar holder in a property, it will make common management extremely difficult and destroy the benefits of ownership in common. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression 'other co shari ners ' in clause (fourthly) of section 15(1) of Punjab Pre emption Act, 1913 is rendered redundant. [126A] 2. In the present case, the appellant seeks to exercise the right of pre empt, conferred on him by that provision. The Courts below have negatived this contention solely on the ground that it cannot stand after the pronouncement of this Court in the case of Jagdish 's case. [127B C] 3. The purport of Atam Prakash 's decision was to deny the right to those relative or relatives of the vendor or vendors who were specified in the erstwhile first three clauses of section15(1), even if they happen to be co shar holders. The expressions 'other than 'in clause fourthly conveys the possibility of their being co shar er also. What this Court disapproved as offen sive to Articles 14 and 15 is the classification based on consanguinity and not on co ownership. [128C D] 4.

The appellants, who were the original plaintiffs in a suit for title and injunction, filed an application under Order 23, rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure, for possession and injunction. The Trial Court granted a decree for possession of the entire property of the appellants. On appeal, the High Court held that once the court was satisfied that there was a compromise, it was for the Court to record the same and no option lay before the Court. In this appeal by special leave, it is contended on behalf of the appel lants that the alienees had no interest in the property prior to the compromise and the alienation was not valid and the transferees had become owners of the property and had even maintained that there were agreements for sale prior to compromise. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The alienees have no interest therein. Their possession is without authority of law. Ordinarily, they would have been liable to account for mesne profits. In view of the fact that there has been a allegation of payment and has become owners, the alienee has no interest. [541B] 1.2 A similar question arose before this Court in Bhoja Govinda Maikap & Anr. vs Janaki Dei & Ors., AIR (1980) Ori. 108 wherein it was held that when a party to the suit is present in court and he has no interests in the land to part with in view of a stipulation in the compromise that on receipt of Rs. 1 lakh he relinquished his entire interest in tho property, the Court must pass an order accordingly.

The appellant company was granted sick leave with effect from December 14, 1969. The workmen were paid dearness allowance at the rate of Rs. 900 per month. The company applied for and obtained special leave to appeal as aforesaid. The Industrial Tribunal held that the benefits admissible under the Act in the matter of grant of sick leave are such as to justify rejection of the workmen 's demand and set aside the award in that respect. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant company that the benefit of sick Leave granted to the workers should not be extended to the workmen because they had benefited a lot under the entire scheme of the Act and it would not be reasonable and proper to confer any additional benefit on them. HELD: (i) The Industrial Court was justified in its view that the workmen are entitled to 7 days sick leave at the time of the commencement of the industrial dispute. [83 E] (ii) The Tribunal was justified, in granting the additional benefits mentioned above. [84 D] (iii) The scheme of benefits admissible to the employees under the Industrial Disputes Act is not a bar to the demand of the workman for sick leave. The benefit granted by the Tribunal are not similar to those admissible under section 56 of the , and the workmen would adversely affect the economy or the indus trial peace, or lead to imbalance in the conditions of service in other industrial establishments. [85 E] In the instant case, the Tribunal was right in holding that the workers were entitled to seven days sick Leave with wages on full emoluments during the period of workman 's physical incapacity to earn their normal wages because of his sickness. It is not necessary in the circumstances of the case to award the benefit to the appellant workmen for it was taken away under the mistaken impression that it had been adequately replaced by the new provisions on the coming into force of the . [85 G H] (iv) The award of the Industrial Tribunal in the present case, therefore, is set aside and the award of Rs 10,000 is restored.

The appellant was detained under sub clause (a) of section 3 of the , with a view to preventing him from acting in any manner prejudicial to the relations of India with the Portuguese Government. The grounds of detention were served on him along with the order of detention and he filed an affidavit explaining the allegations against him. He also stated that he was not aware of the grounds of his detention as required by section 7 of the Act. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the grounds did not contain any particulars nor did they state any particulars of the activities alleged to have been carried on by the petitioner. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The grounds cannot be considered to be vague merely because they are vague as to hamper him in his right to make a representation under article 22(5). [391 F] (ii)The question whether or not the grounds furnished were vague must depend on the facts of each case. If the detaining authority is under a constitutional obligation to furnish reasonably definite grounds, as well as adequate particulars then and there, or shortly thereafter. But the right of the detenue to be furnished particulars is subject to the limitation under article 21. [391 G] (iii)The requirement of section 7(1) of the has to be read in the light of the circumstances of each particular case. The right of a detenue to have his representation considered against public interest cannot be said to be implicit or implicit in such a situation. [392 C D] (iv)In the present case there was no reason for disagreeing with the conclusion reached by the detaining Authority that what was stated in the affidavit was not vague. There is nothing to suggest that this question was not considered by the authority at the time when the grounds were furnished.

The respondent was a commissioned officer in the Indian Army and was attached to the Army Ordnance Corps Training Centre. He was charged with having committed acts of gross misconduct. The allegations were that he committed acts prejudicial to the maintenance of discipline, while as a result thereof, he was suspended from service. The Chief of the Army Staff, after going through the proceedings of the Court of Inquiry held in his favour and after going into the proceedings, found him guilty of the charges framed against him. He filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the order of removal from service on the ground that r. 14 of the Defence Rules, 1954, was ultra vires the . The High Court dismissed the petition holding that r 14 of Army Rules, 1955, was intra vires the , and that the action taken thereunder was without authority. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) Rule 14 of Indian Army Rules is not ultra vires. It is a rule which is in derogation of section 45 of the . Rule 14 is an independent power. Although section 19 uses the words "subject to the provisions of this Act" it speaks of removal of a person from the service. Section 20 provides that on conviction by Court martial an officer is liable to be cashiered or to suffer such less punishment as is in this Act mentioned. [450 H] (ii) The power under section 19 is an alternative to the power to make rules providing for the removal from the Service of persons subject to the Act. It follows that there may be a valid rule where under, subject to other provisions of the Act, the Central Government may remove a person in derogation Of the provisions Of section 45. But the power under s.19 is an additional power. [451 B C] (iii) The words " subject to" in section 19 make section 19 subject to section 45 and the Central Govern ment has no power to remove a persons from the ' service. Rule 14, therefore, is ultra vires as it is not intra vires.

The appellant was a Panchayat Samiti under the Bombay Village Panchayats Act, 1958. The respondent filed an application under article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court for a writ quashing the resolution dated February 25, 1963 passed by the Standing Committee on April 1, 1964 and directing that the octroi duty be levied on all goods coming into its local limits as per the Schedule to the Act. The High Court held that the Panchayat could not dismiss the appeal as being barred by limitation because it was filed within 60 days of the date of the resolution. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Standing Committee was entitled to deal with the appeal on merits. [217 B] (ii) The resolution dated April 1. 1964 was passed an essential condition precedent to the levy of octroi duty. The Panchayat could validly impose octroi duty and it could be imposed and collected with effect from January 14, 1964. He says that this point was raised before the Full Bench in the case of R.S. Dang vs State of Bombay ; , and the High Courts held that it was not necessary for the Panchayat to fix the octroi limits in accordance with law. [218 C] (iii) The word " octroi" is used in a wide sense, and includes all kinds of taxes which are imposed and the rate at which it is levied. Under r. 3(b), what the panchayat does is to consider objections and suggestions and then finally make the choice as regards two things, i.e., the tax or fee to be levied and (2) that if the octroi is finally decided to levy any tax or fees, the rules in that Part shall apply to the imposition of taxes and the rates at which they are to be imposed. [220 D E] (iv) The High Courts have implied that this was not a case where there was no sufficient cause for issuing the notification under r.3(b).

The appellants were prosecuted under section 31(1) read with section 33(1). The appellants contended that the conciliation proceedings could be prolonged only when the report of the Conciliation Officer was received by the appropriate Government and that as 14 days had expired before March 18, 1952, the dismissal could not be said to be one within the meaning of section 12(6) of the Act. Held, that the provisions of sub section 2 Of section 20 of the , are applicable only when a report is received by an appropriate Government. The conciliation proceedings therefore do not end when the reports under section 12 (6) are made by the Conciliation officer but when that report is receives by the Government, the appropriate government has to make its report within 14 days of the commencement of the conciliation proceeding or within such shorter period fixed by the State Government. Colliery Mazdoor Congress, Asansol vs New Beerbhoom Coal Co., Ltd., ; , referred to. The provisions of section 20(2)(b) of Act 2 Of 1952 are applicable to all conciliation proceedings whether in regard to utility services or otherwise. All conciliation proceedings under this sub section shall be deemed to have concluded in the case where no settlement is reached, when the Report of the Advisory Officer is received and the report is sent by the Inspector to the appropriate Govern ment. Colliery Labour Union Asanso vs Newerson Bissur Railway Co., , referredto. The Act does not affect the jurisdiction of the Industrial Tribunal under section 20 (2)(a) of that Act.

The petitioner was detained under the provisions of the , by an order dated 2nd January, 1983 passed by the respondent No. 1 under section 3(2) of the . The grounds of detention were that on 24th December 1985 between 10th and 11th January 1986 the subject matter of the incident had been referred to a committee constituted for the purpose of enquiry into the exchange of fire between two rival groups. The petitioner was arrested when he was released on bail in pursuance of an order passed by this Court on 2nd February, 1986. On the question whether the detention order was justified or not, HELD: (1) The grounds for forming the satisfaction for the need for the detention were there, and there was rational nexus between the object of the order as contemplated by the Act and the materials on record. [910C] (2) It is well settled in the constitutional framework that the power of directing preventive detention given to the appropriate authorities must be exercised in exceptional cases as contemplated under the various provisions of different statutes dealing with preventive detention and should be used with great deal of circumspection. There must be awareness of the facts necessitating preventive custody of a person for social defence. If a man is in custody and there is no imminent possibility of his being released, the power to preventive detention should not be exercised. [936F G] (3) The order of preventive detention when it was passed was not invalid and on relevant considerations, the service of the impugned order was not on proper consideration. It may be mentioned that in the affidavit filed by the District Magistrate, the detaining authority, it has been stated that the activities of the petitioner 's brother and the petitioner have disturbed the normal tempo of life in Katras and Jogta Police Station in Dhanbad area. The incidents alleged were created a terror and not only law and order problem but problem of public order. [961F G; 910A B] (4) It was also stated that there was a statement to the effect that the petitioner was in jail and was likely to be enlarged on bail. But on what consideration that opinion was expressed is not indicated especially in view of the fact that the detenu was detained in a murder charge in the background of the circumstances mentioned before. His application for bail could have been opposed on cogent materials before the Court of Justice. [963B C] (5) The detention order, therefore, is set aside.

The respondent assessee firm manufactures gold bars, i.e., manufacturers of shroffs and dealers in gold. The assessee firm manufactured gold bars and sold them to the dealers. The Sales Tax Officer assessed the respondent firm under section 28 of the Gold Control Act, 1968 on the ground that it suffered from the vice of excessive delegation of legislative power inasmuch as no criteria or guide lines have been provided by reference to which the power conferred on the Administrator to refuse permission or grant permission should be exercised and that the section confers an arbitrary and uncanalised power upon the Administrator. The High Court struck down sec. 28 of Act, 1969 as it stood prior to its amendment by the Amending Act No. 26 of 1969, constitutionally invalid on the grounds that it suffers from the infirmity of excessive delega tion of legislative powers inasmuch as the restrictions which have been imposed in section 28 are meant to prevent circumvention of other provisions of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The object and reasons for exercising the power of discretion conferred on an Administrator by sec. 26(6) in several of its clauses referred to certain concepts which Administrator was required to take into account, and these concepts were regarded as indefinite, uncertain and vague. [955C] 1.2 In the instant case, the objective, the policy and the scheme of the enactment together with the necessity to ensure prevention of circumvention Of the other provisions is clearly inapplicable. The object, therefore, is not to provide any blanket or absolute prohibition upon a dealer from carrying on money lending, banking or any other business in the same premises in which he carries on business as a dealer but he is prevented only from carrying out business as money lender or banker on the security of any article, ornament or both unless authorised by the administrator. Even the restriction imposed by sec 28 is not absolute in as much as the Administrator can authorise the third person to carry on the business in licensed premises of the dealer and while implementing such limited restrictions or granting relief against the same he will be guided by the policy, and purposes of the act in making his orders. [936F G] Harakchand Ratanchand Banthia vs Asst. Collector of Central Excise, Poona, ; , followed. 1.3 The object of the Urban Ceiling Act is to provide for the acquisition of goods lending, Banking or any kind of foreign business, for the control of production, manufacture, supply distribution, use and possession of and business in gold ornaments and articles of gold and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto. [951B] Harkchand Ratan Chand Banthia & Ors. vs Union of India & Ors., ; , referred to. 1:4 The object is not the same as the administrator can have to make judicious use of his power or discretion and any improper exercise is liable to be corrected by a higher authority. If that be so it cannot be said that unfettered or uncanalised or arbitrary power has been conferred upon the Administration under sec. 24(6).

The appellants were appointed trustees of a temple by the Manager of a Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments, L. R. Act, 1951, in respect of certain properties belonging to the temple. The appellants filed an application before the Magistrate under section 87 of the Act for possession of the properties. The Magistrate held that the lands belonged to the deity and that the alienees were entitled to the possession of those properties. On appeal, the High Court held that as the alienors had been appointed trustees by respondent No. 1, the appellants could not be said to have acquired title by adverse possession before 12 years from the date of the alienations. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the suit was barred by limitation under article 134 B of the Indian Limitation Act; and (2) the appellants had acquired title to the properties by prescription, and that as they were entitled only to the property belonging to them, the suit must be dismissed. HELD: (i) The question whether the alienee was a trustee or not is irrelevant for the purpose of article 134B. [133 B] Gnanasambanda vs C.I.T., L.R. , referred to. (ii) In order that a plea can be raised it must be shown that a part of the property belonged to him and not to the religious endowment.
