The question as to whether on facts proved in this case, an inference can be drawn from the fact proved in the present case, is one which was irrelevant for determining the question. [134 C] G. Narayan Das vs State of Orissa, ; , referred by the High Courts to. In the instant case, the alienor was still alive and so it thought that the plea of adverse possession could not he sustained. The suit had been brought against respondents 1 to 3 on the date when they were appointed Trustees of the temple and other persons who were acting as de facto managers of the trust. [135 D] G, Narayan Das & Ors. vs State, ; and Damodar Das & Anr. vs Smt. Rama Devi & Ors., ; , distinguished.

The appellant, who was the owner of a cinema theatre in the State of Jammu and Kashmir, had filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the legality and validity of the orders passed by the District Magistrate and the appellate authority under the Jammu & Kashmir (Cinematograph) Act, 1989. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the renewal of the licence could not be made in the name of any party other than the original licensee, so long as there had not been any transfer of the license by the original licensees to another with the sanction of the licensing authority. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that even though the licence had been granted in favour of Ved Gupta and not in favour M/s. Krishan Kumar, the license was still subsisting and that the license having been granted by the competent authority in favour the appellant, he did not have the possession of the premises and therefore could not claim a renewal of his licence. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order passed by District Magistrate directing the suspension of the cinema shows in the Theatre cannot be said to have visited the writ petitioners with any adverse civil consequences. They had no legal right whatever to conduct the cinema show in the theatre without a licence in contravention of the law. [582B] 2.1 The High court was wrong in holding that since the license granted by M/S. Ved Gupta was in favour a partnership consisting of himself and his partners, it necessarily follows that where the licensed premises including the cinematograph used therein belonged to a partnership and one of the partners obtains a licence, in his individual capacity, he alone is the licensee. [591C D] 2:2 The license granted in respect of the Apsara Theatre was in the nature of a licence for the premises permanently equipped for cinematograph exhibition in the appellant Nagar Nagar, Jammu and Nagar, and that it necessarily followed that where a licensed premises includes the partnership, the other partners automatically acquire interest in the licence and that in the absence of any legal right or legitimate expectation being available to the petitioners, there was no obligation on the part of the District Magis trate to afford them a hearing before passing the impugned order. [592F G] 2(a) The High Courts have consistently taken the view that where an application for a licence is made by a partnership firm and one or more partners obtains licences in his separate name, the others automatically acquire interests in the licensee and that such rights are granted to them in his personal and individual capacity. [593B C] (b) In the instant case, the licence was granted by District Magi trate in favour Apsar Mal, the appellant. The licence was a valid one and the license could not have been cancelled on the ground of its being the sole licensee. The impugned order was therefore violative of principles of natural justice. [595C D; 594D] (c) The impugned orders were passed by a District Magistrate in exercise of his function of administering the provisions of the Act and the Rules and the implied power to take all steps necessary for effective enforcement of the statute. [596F G]. (d) The order was not one suspending the licence issued in respect thereof. It was only the licensee who had no authority in law to conduct such exhibition of films. There was no suspension of a license issued in favour B, and the impugned orders passed against him were therefore illegal.

The appellants were displaced persons and on 30 8 1952 the respondent entered into an agreement with them, for the purchase of the stock of raw materials, unsold finished goods, spare parts, cars etc. which were in the mills and the factory in question was leased to the appellants for a period of five years on the terms and conditions set out therein. The appellants were put in possession of the mills on 31 8 1952. On 12 2 1954 the respondent issued a notice to the appellant under section 12 Of the , terminating the lease, and the appellants filed an application before the respondent for a writ of certiorari for quashing the notice, contending that section 12 was ultra vires the powers of the Custodian under that section and that the notice was ultra rites. The High Court held that section had no authority under section 10 to issue any directions with reference thereto and that section 10 applied only to leases granted by the evacuee and not by the Custodian himself and that there was no warrant for imposing a further limitation on that section that that lease should also have been granted by an evacuee. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The respondent was acting within his authority in issuing the notice under section 13 Of the Act. Under section 12 of the , the Custodian had the power to cancel a lease granted by him and not to the Custodian. The operative portion of the section which confers power on the Custodian to cancel the lease does not by implication repeal statutes conferring rights on lessees, and cannot prevail as against them and has been inserted ex abundanti cautela. Aswini Kumar Ghosh vs Arabinda Bose, , 21 24 S.C.R. 884, followed. (ii) The provisions of section 12 are intended to repel a possible contention that section 13 does not apply to leases granting by the evacuees and cannot override a bar imposed by any law but only applies to leases in respect of which certain directions were given. As Arabinda Ghosh vs Mullick A. Irani, ; , followed.

The respondent was a minor son of the appellant. The Sub Divisional Officer, Hanumangarh, by his order dated 10th August, 1972 determined the ceiling area for the appellant in respect of his father and allotted him to the respondent. The respondent filed an appeal before the Revenue Appellate Authority which allowed the same on the ground that the appellant was in possession of 112 Bighas only and not 129 Bighas and 3 Biswas as held by the lower courts. In a revision application preferred by the respondent, the Board of Revenue set aside the order of the Sub Divisional officer on the grounds that the petitioner was in posses sion of 112 bighas only and that he was in pos session of 112. Bighas even though he was only 13 years of age when the ceiling proceedings were finalised by the Sub Divi sional Officer on 5th May, 1976. The Board went on to hold that there is no provision for separate units in Chapter III B of the Act of 1955 and dismissed the revision application filed by the appellant under section 230 of the Rajasthan Tenancy Act, 1973. In the writ petition filed before the High Court, the respondent contended that no appeal having been filed by him against the order, the said order became final and the Board had no jurisdiction to set aside that part of the sub Divisional Officer 's order which had gone against the State and in his favour. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Section 221 of the Indian Tenancy Act provides for executive powers of superintendence and control over all revenue courts. It is open to the Board to exercise its powers of supervision on all its subordinate courts in order to regulate the functioning of 'the subordinate courts so as to keep them within their respective spheres of jurisdiction. If the subordinate court disregards any specific provision of law and does something illegal it is open for the Board or Revenue to interfere and set the matter right. A similar question arose before this Court in Kana and others vs Board of revenue, Rajasthan, ILR [1973] 1 S.C.R. 884 (F.B.) and Kana and Others vs Board Of Revenue, Rajasthan; ILR [1974] 1 All. E.R., 981 (F). In the instant case, the appellant had been in possession on 14th March, 1963 and was only thirteen years of old age when he was admittedly minor son. The order passed by the Board was set aside by the High Courts. [726C D] 2.1 There is no restriction on the powers of the Board under section 221 of Indian Evidence Act to set at naught the judicial orders of the courts. [ 728D E] 2:2 There is nothing illegal in law in the order dated 14th April, 1975 passed by a subordinate court. The appellant had not filed an application for adducing additional evidence in support of his contention.

The first respondent, a journalist, was employed as an advocate in the newspaper establishments. The first respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the notice served on it by the Deputy Labour Commissioner, Nagpur, calling upon it to implement the orders of the Central Government made under section 12 of the Act. The High Court accepted the plea of the first respondent and declared that the law reports published in the newspapers were not newspapers within the meaning of section 2(b) of the . In appeal to this Court, on behalf of the appellant it was contended that the Law reports published by the first Respondent are not newspapers as defined in the Act and therefore the order made by the Central Govern ment on the basis of the recommendations of the Palekar Tribunal is unsustainable. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The law reports which are being published by a Ist respondent are reports of recent decisions of the highest court of the land. [785B] 2.1 The law report which is being published from Delhi which publishes the judgments rendered by the High Courts in India is not sufficient to hold that the laws report do not carry any news and that the public is not interested in them. [783F] 2:2 In the instant case, the first respond ent, All India Reporter Limited, publisher of law reports in the interests of their own business vie ws. The First Respondent, All Indian Reporter Limited and other publishers of law report in the interest of their business vies, are publishers and editorials.

The appellant was a monthly tenant of the suit premises. He continued to occupy the premises for five years and thereafter filed ejectment proceedings against him under section 41(1)(a) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947. The appellant contended that he was a licensee and not a sub tenant. The trial court decreed the ejectment petition holding that the appellant had failed to prove that he had been a subtenant of the respondent and that the Court of Small Causes had no jurisdiction to deal with the eviction petition. On appeal, the High Court held that the respondent was a tenant of a monthly tenancy and therefore it was recorded that as agreed by the parties, the leave and licence agreement between the parties was renewed. The High Court also held that in view of the legal position and also the fact that the rent light bill stood in the name of the appellant showed that there was no desire to create any lease by the document mentioned therein and the appellant regarded him as a mere licensee. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 In order to get the advantage of section 15A of the Act, the occupant must be in occupation by permission of the grantor that after the recovery of the permission a suit for possession could have been instituted under section41(1) of Bombay Rent and licence Agreement which expired on 31st March 1966. [1065B] 1.2 In order that an agreement creates a lease rather than a licence, it is necessary to determine whether a document created a lease or not. The intention of the parties is the real test for ascertaining the character of a document. The solution that would seem to have been found is, as one would expect, that it must depend on the intention of both the parties. [1165C D] 1:3. In orderto get the benefit of section15A of Bombay Rents Act, 1949, the occupants must be, in occupation, by permission, of the grantee, who had a subsisting agreement on the 1st of February 1973, then he did not get the protection of the amended provision of the said Act. [1266D] 2.1 The intention is the actual test for determining the character or transaction. The solutions that would appear to have existed are as one will expect, and circumstances might be established which negative the intention to create a lease. This Court in Errington vs Erringle, ; , referred to. 1:4. In deciding whether an agreement created between the par ties the relationship of landlord and tenant or merely that of licensor and licensee is enough, the court has to look at the intention with due care and caution and the trial court should not exercise jurisdiction under Article 227 of the Constitution over such decision. [1366E F] 2:5. The test of exclusive possession was important because the intention was the real criterion for ascertaining whether a particular document created one or the licensee as defined in section 5(4A) on the Ist of February, 1973. If he was such a licensee, the non obstante clause of section 105 would give him the status and protection of a tenant in spite of there being anything to the contrary in any other law or in contract. But if he was not a licensee under a subsisting contract on the first day of February. 1973 then he could not get his advantage of the amendment of section 5 (4A). [1367G H] 2 :6. The question whether an application for eviction filed by the respondent under section 21 of the Rent Act is a monthly or licence or not, depends upon the intention and the Trial Court has taken one view which is a possible and plausible view merely because another view is attractive, the trial Court has took one view and it cannot be said that the view taken by the High court or the Court was incorrect.

The respondent was a Ruler of the former Dholpur State. He was assessed to excise duty under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, on the ground that he had been assessed to income tax for the year 1947 48 and 1949 49. The respondent contended that the Ruler had no authority to levy any tax on the income tax as it emerged from the Covenanting State which came into existence after August 15, 1947, and that the United State of Rajasthan was a new sovereign and was not bound by any obligation imposed upon him by the new sovereign. Held, that the definition of "Government of the United States" in article 295(2) of the Constitution is wide enough to include the Government of the corresponding Indian State as it was on January 26, 1950 or would also include all the former States which came to be merged into it through the process to which the new State had been formed. The Ruler of Rajasthan merged with the United state of Rajasthan and thus became a sovereign and could not be said to have intended to respect all the rights flowing from laws so continued and assumed all liabilities arising from the existence of those laws. The new sovereign throughout the territory of India was entitled to levy tax on income tax in accordance with the agreement between the Ruler and the Ruler. The United State merged into the United Dominion of India as a result of the Covenant entered into by it with the Government and there was no recognition of liability by the old sovereign or the new Government. The State of Jaipur vs Stale of Rajasthan, ; , followed.

The appellant was a dealer in the sale and groundnut to the State Government. The State Government issued a notification under section 3 of the Madras Commercial Crops Markets Act, 1933, directing the constitution of a market committee at Virudhunagar, for the purchase and sale of commercial crops in the State of Madras and for that purpose to establish markets and make rules for their proper administration. The appellant challenged the validity of the provisions of the Act on the ground that they infringed articles 19(1)(f) and 31 of the Constitution. Held, that the provisions Of section 5 of the impugned Act were not violative of article 19(i)(f). The object of the legislation was to protect the producers of crops, particularly commercial crops, from exploitation by them and to secure better living conditions in the country. The Act did not provide for any restriction on the right to do business unless it was clearly established that the provision was too drastic and unreasonable so as to defeat the very purpose of the law. The provisions of section 5 were not only reasonable restrictions but also tend to defeat its object. The impugned provisions did not contravene article 19 (i)(g) or (g). The Act was an integrated one, and it regulates the buying and selling of commercial crop and the bulk of transactions in such markets are regulated by the provisions contained in the Act. The fact that the growers may be under some difficulties in this regard does not affect the validity or otherwise of the scheme of the statute. The object is to protect them from being exploited by unscrupulous traders, who do business in the market established and run by them. The growing of commodities for money, the business of buying and sale and the purchase of goods at fair prices are regulated and controlled by the rules made under the Act and no restrictions on the fundamental rights of the petitioners can be justified as they are not prohibited from holding their property as property. The levy of sales tax is not a trade allowance within the meaning of section 14 of the , but only an allowable deduction under that section. The contention that the appellants in C. No. 169 of 1955 were running the market as an occupation or business with high standards and that they were not prevented from doing their business for they could still be utilised for commodities other than those specified in the explanation is without substance. The definition of "trade" in section 2(f) of the Indian , includes trade allowance, which has been defined to mean a charge levied at a fixed rate for goods or goods specified in a notified area for the purpose of carrying on the business established by the Market Committee. The appellants were running a market as a dealer and were selling commodities at proper rates. The notification directing the establishment of a Market Committee was not invalid because it had no reasonable relation to the object which the legislature sought to achieve. The exemption granted under section 5(1) of Act was not only a trade allowances but also an allowable allowance under the bye law.

The appellant was convicted for murder and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the sentence of death but reduced it to transportation for life. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The conviction must be maintained. There is no evidence that the appellant was guilty of murder or that he had committed the murder. It is not enough as in the present case the appellant did not have any motive to kill the deceased and his father. The circumstances showed that there was no prior meeting of minds to form a pre arranged plan. [1090 B] (ii) There was no evidence of any prior meeting. There was nothing to connect the appellant with the crime. He had only asked for a number of persons who were not present in the village and wanted to tell them what had happened. The mere fact that he did not ask for a person to be present, would not have the common intention required by section 326 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. [1189 C] (iii) There is nothing to show that there were any prior meetings. It was only when the appellant asked for the first time to have passed the test in his favour that he could have done anything except be present and even if it be accepted that he was willing to kill a given individual, he cannot be convicted of the murder so as to attract section 149. [1102 D] (iv) The evidence showed that the deceased had been attacked by the appellant and the other two who did not say that they were present and that there had been no previous meeting. It could not be said that the second meeting was a pre fixed arranged plan, but it was only a case of murder and not of an axe.

The petitioner was a Sub Inspector of Central Public Works Department under the Ministry of Works and Housing in Government of India. He was compulsorily retired by an order dated 3.8.1976 with effect from 5.11.76 made under Rule 56(j)(i) of Fundamental Rules. The petitioner challenged that order before the High Court on the ground that he was an officiating Sub Inspector in Class II service and was compulsorily retire by exercising the power under Rule 57(j) of the Fundamental Rules, as he had not at all been retired from service on 5.10.1976. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the petitioner was an officer who was in Class I or Class II Service or post even when he held a post of either class substantively or temporarily or on officiating basis and therefore, on the date of the order he had completed the age of 54 years. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that as the petitioner had not attained the age Of 55 years by the date he had attained the maximum age of 50 years, he could have retired from serv ice with effect only from 5th November 1976 and, therefore, he cannot be deemed to have been compulsorily retired under sub clause (i). Dismissing the writ Petition, this Court, HELD: 1. Rule 56 (j) is meant to cover only those who are in a post on a regular basis, i.e., in a substantive capacity, and not on an officiating basis only. [638C] 2. The possibility of a reversion to the substantive post is not germane to the exercise of power contained in F.R. 56(1)(i). The purpose of Fundamental Rule 56 is to confer power on the appropriate authority to compulsorily retire Government servant in the public interest and the classification of Government servants into two categories covered by sub clauses (i) and (ii) has a purpose behind it. If the condi tions indicated in sub clause(i) is satisfied, namely, the Government servant is in Class 1 or Class I service or post, the benefit must substantively belong to the two classes of service or posts cannot be introduced into the scheme. The purpose is to classify Gov ernment servants into three categories and sub cl.(i) takes within its sweep those Government servants who at the relevant time are in Class 11 service or on substantive basis. [625E F] 3.

The respondents, who were the husband of respondent No. 1 and father of respondent Nos. 2 to 5, filed a suit against the appellant Corporation for recovery of Rs. 50,000 on the ground that the medical examination report was not submitted by the doctor in charge of the deceased and that the deceased had fulfilled his part of the insurance contract and the appellant corporation had encashed the cheques issued towards premium payable by the deceased. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that there was no concluded contract. On appeal, the High Court held that the respondents were entitled to claim the amount along with interest at six per cent per annum from the date of refusal of payment till the date on which the demand was made and that it was not necessary for them to have any cause of action. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the proposal was not accepted and as such there was a concluded contract between the deceased 's husband and the Corporation. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was in error in holding that the plea that Divisional Manager was the only authority to accept had not been categorically taken in the written statement filed on behalf the appellant. On the other hand, there was an express provision in the Financial Powers Act, 1960 dealing with the financial powers. Indeed there was nothing in the Act which would justify a conclusion of the High court that there is a concluded agreement. The expression "underwrite" signifies acceptance by some act or acts agreed on by the parties or from which the law raises a presumption of acceptance. [359E F] In the instant case, the appellant had not filed any evidence of any order prohibiting other officers one step below in rank, in this case the Assistant Divisional Manager, to exercise the power of Divisional Manager. The Trial Court was therefore right in holding the appellant guilty of the charge and that he should have been acquitted. [360F G] 2.1 In view of the fact that such a long time has elapsed and further in view of finding that the payment of first premium would amount to acceptance of the proposal, the plea of Divisional manager being a mere formality is accepted. Acceptance must be signified by some acts or acts con cerned on by parties or through their agents from which it is possible and communicates his acceptance to the person making the offer. Whether the final acceptance is that of the assured or insurers, however, depends simply on the way in which negotiations for an insurance have progressed.

The appellants applied for an interim injunction restraining the Bank of India from taking any steps in pursuance of a letter of credit opened in favour of M/s. V. L. R. 60 IA. 76. The trial court granted an interim order restraining encashment of the letters of credit pending disposal of the suit. In appeal, the High Court set aside the order and remanded the case to the trial court for trial. On remand, the trial Court passed a decree in favour and directed the appellant to take steps in execution of the decree. The High Court held that an order granting interim injunction was a final order as far as this Court is concerned and that it was not necessary for the High Courts to give any direction to grant interim injunction. In the appeal by special leave, HELD: (1) An order passed by the High court in appeal which does not finally dispose of a suit or proceeding and leave the rights and obligations of the parties for determination in the suit or proceedings from which appeal has arisen is not final within the meaning of article 133(1)(a) and (b). The expression "final order" in section 205 of the Government of India Act, 1935, means an interlocutory order passed in a proceeding. [701 B C] (2) An interim injunction cannot be granted unless it is final. In a suit pending before the High 'Court, an order deciding that circumstances had not been established such as would justify an order for stay of execution of a decree under appeal was not a final decision on the rights of the party in dispute in the suits or proceeding. If after the order is made, the suit is still left alive and has got to be tried, and the rights in disputes have to be determined, the order being interlocutory. [700 C D] (3) The expression 'final order ' in section 206 of the Code of Civil Procedure means a final adjudication on the merits of the dispute in a suit. An order under section 205 is an interlocutory one and is final within its meaning. [601 G H] Ramchand Manjimal vs Goverdhandas Vishindas Ratan Chand, ; , followed. (4) The order refusing to grant an interim relief did not determine the rights or obligations of parties in relation to the matter in dispute. [071 C D]. Mohanlal Maganlal Thakkar vs State of Gujarat, A.I.R. 1958 S.C. 1017, referred to.

The respondent assessee, a manufacturer of cotton fabrics, was manufacturing cloth in the hands of the processor. The process of manufacture was done by the assessee and the process of manufac turing was done through job work. The assessee claimed that the assessable value of the processed fabric would be the value of grey cloth in his hands and not the value at which he would get the fabrics manufactured in the market, that the valuation should be adopted on the basis of the price at which the said manufacturer would be selling the processed goods in the factory gate for the processing on job work basis. The Assistant Collector rejected the claim on the ground that the transaction was not a sale under the Act and that the value would be only the price paid by the processor to the processor, and that he had no intention to evade the duty under the said Act. On appeal, the Appellate Collector held that the assessee was liable to pay excise duty under Item No. 174 of the Central Excise Tariff. The Revenue filed an appeal before the Customs, Excise & Gold (Control) Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal rejected the contention of the assessee that the market value of processed fabric should be the price of the grey cloth and not that the processor 's profits would be included in the price charged by the manufacturer. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the cost of processing should be taken as the assessablevalue of the finished fabric and excise duty would be charged to the fabric on that basis provided that the declaration as to the price, at which it is selling the goods must be the valuation of under the Central Act and the rules made thereunder. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The assessable value for the processed fabrics should be determined on the price which would be taken by the Excise authorities as the valuation at which they are selling the said goods. [346B] 1.2 In order to explain the position it is made clear by the following illustration: if the trader who entrusts cotton or man made fabric to the processing for processing on the job work is required relating to the prices at which such manufacturer is selling, the said good and the person so authorised agrees to discharge all the liabili ty under the aforesaid Act and rules made therein. The price at the factory, gate or deemed to be the prices of the goods plus the value thereof, the manufacturing profit and expenses but not any other subsequent profit or expenses. [347C D] 1:3. In order that the goods owned by one person are manufactured by another, the information is required for explaining the position. It is necessary to include the processor in the assessable price of processed fabrics and excise duties would be chargeable to the manufacturer on that footing provided that he has the intention to discharge the duty of under section 3 of the Act. [349D] 2. The cost of process should be calculated on the value which at the time of filing the fabric and the goods manufactured by the processing agency plus the manufacturing profits and the manufacturing expenses but cannot be included as the cost price at where the assessee who entrustles cotton or manufacture to the processed cloth for processing, because those would be post manufacturing profits.

The appellant was appointed as a clerk on June 1, 1963 by the Panchayat Samiti, Loharu. He was confirmed in that post in course of time. On March 14, 1975 he was promoted as a Head Clerk on an ad hoc basis. On April 1, 1975, he was again promoted as Head Clerk. The Punjab Government notified the absorption of the appellant as a Clerk though as stated earlier he was working as a head clerk in the Loharam Panchayat Samiti. He filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging his absorption on a lower post. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the appellant was entitled to continue in the service of the Panchayat on the same terms and conditions on which he was employed by the Government. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the State that by reason of section 14(4) of the Punjab Panchayat Samitis and Zilla Parishads (Haryana Amendment) Act, 1973, the Panchayat Samitis were divested of their power to make appointments to the Panchayats. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appointment of the appel lant to the post of a Head clerk prior to his absorption in Government service had to be recognised and protected, despite the fact that such appointment was made after June 13, 1973 when the Amending Act came into force. There is no substance in this contention. Even assuming for the purposes of argument that the right to be considered for promotion is a term and condition of service, what is relevant for our purpose is not whether the appellant is entitled to be promoted as an Assistant or a Head Clerks. He is appointed lawfully to the posts of a Clerk and that is the post in which the Government has absorbed him. [738C D] 2. The appellant was promoted on ad hoc appointment prior to June 13. 1975, but he was not confirmed in the Government service. Since the appellant had been appointed without the authority of law, the Government was not bound to absorb him in the post. [750D E] 3. Even if it is assumed for the purpose of argument, that the rights to be consti tuted are a term, and condition is of service what is applicable for our purposes is not that the appell lant was entitled as he was appointed lawfully. He had been promoted as Assistant or Head Clerk in any event. But, as a result of the deletion of section 33 of the Act by the Amending act of 1973, he became entitled to continued in the serv ice of the Government on the date on which it purported to do so.

The appellants, who were the disciple of a Math Sauna and were the Mahant, filed a suit claiming that the property in dispute belonged to the Math Saunti. The trial court decreed the suit but included a finding in his judgment that Sadashiv Yati was not a regularly constituted Mahant of Math Saana. On appeal by the plaintiffs, the High Court allowed both the appeals and held that the Amauli properties had been purchased by the Math, and that the income from the properties belonged to Math or the deity. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that where a nucleus of dedicated property exists, the acquisition of additional property should be attributed to the application of the nuclea and must therefore be regarded as property belonging to the math or the temple of the Mahant. HELD: (i) The fund from which the Ama corpus properties were acquired constituted the personal property of Mahant Shivshankar Yati. On his death in 1917, all those properties and wealth devolved on him from his predecessor Shivs Shankar Yati and he was granted a succession certificate by the District Judge, Ghazipur in respect of the two fixed deposits made by Mahant Shiv Sher Yati in the Bank of Bengal. Mahant Shiv shankar Yat is not a mere fact that a Mohunt is an ascetic does not raise any presumption that a property in his possession is not his personal property. [663 H] (ii) The income from properties belonging to Math and the deity left any appreciable surplus after meeting the expenditure on account of bhog, arpan, deepdan, daily and annual puja and the other obligations specified in the waqf deed. [665 B C] Gurcharan Prasad vs Krishnanand, ; , referred to.

The appellants who were displaced persons from West Pakistan were allotted certain quasi permanent allotments of land in the village of Raikot. The appellants challenged the allotment on the ground that they had been wrongly allotted to them under section 16(1) of the , and that consequently their allotment had been rightly cancelled. Held, that the Custodian bad no power to cancel the allotment. The provisions of section 19(1)(a) and (b) of Act 1 of 1954 were not applicable to a proceeding before an authority created by the . The appellants could not be permitted to make out a new case at this stage of argument because the Custodian had been in possession at the critical time they would have had the right to obtain a permanent transfer in their favour. Held further, that section 19 of the Act was not applicable as it did not apply to a proceedings before an officer created by section 16 of the . Section 19(i) is a general provision and the particular provision regarding cancellation of allotment is section 19 (1) which does not refer to entrustment at all and it is only when there is such a provision that the managing officer or managing corporation has no function to perform with respect to evacuee property. The fact that subsequent to the issue of the notification under section 12(1), the property would cease to be evacuee property, does not make any difference in the result because what is essential is the facts of holding and possession of the land on the date of the Notification. Bal Mukund vs State of Punjab, [1959] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 869, followed.

The State Public Service Commission issued a notification inviting applications from eligible candidates for the post of Upper Zila Basic Shiksha Adhikari (Care ments) District Inspectress of Girls Schools/Associate Regional Dulaji ousalodian of Girls schools in Uttar Pradesh Educational Service Junior Scale (earch) District Inspecto rised by the State Government on May 5, 1985. The recruitment examination was in two stages written and interview/personality test. After the written examina tion was over, a corrigendum was published on June 8, 1985, which was published in the newspapers and was published again on June 9, 1985 and was also published on the same day. The selection process was completed in two stage written and interviews/personals test. The appellant State Public Services Commission rejected the claim of the appellants for re holding the recruitment examination. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 When no defect was pointed out in regard to the written examination and the sole objection was confined to exclusion of a group of successful candidates in the written exami nation, there was no justification for cancelling the written part of the recruitment examina tions. On the other hand, the situation could have been appropriately met by setting aside the recruitment and asking for a fresh interview of all eligible candidates on the basis of the written and the freshly held interview became eligible for selection. [125B C] 1.2 The State Public Serv ices Commission should have been more careful in dealing with the matter so that four years in the process of recruitment would not have been lost and the public cause would not be suffered. Public interest has been appropriately considered by setting down the four year in the instant case. [126C D] 2.1 The State Government should have be more careful to set aside the selection and asking the High Court for a re holding of it. [127D E] 2:2 In the instant cases, when no defect had been pointed out, the High Courts could have directed that the order of the Public Service Com mission cancelling the entire recruitment examination be quashed. The State Commission should also have been less careful in deal ing with the matters so that 4 years in tact would not hav er affected the selection. On account of improper feeding into the computa tion some of the candidates who had better performance in the viva voce were not called and candidates securing lesser marks in the examination were not only called for interview but were also finally selected. When this position was known and upon an inquiry was factually estab lished, the Public Services Com mission should have acted in a more careful manner by setting it aside. [ 127E F] 2 :3 The State of Uttar Pradesh has been properly met by set aside candidates who have better performance.

The appellant filed a suit against the respondent for recovery of possession of the Dera and properties attached to it. The prayer in the plaint was that the appellant be declared an independent Dera as his successor in charge of the Shiromani Dera at Patiala. The trial court decreed the suit. In appeal, the High Court held that after the death of Som Dass, the respondent ceased to be the Mahant of the dera and the appeal could be continued under Q. 22, r. 10 of the Civil Procedure Code against the person upon whom the interest had devolved. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. The suit was filed on the basis that the appel lant as the lawfully appointed mahant was entitled to manage the properties of the respondent. When a suit is brought by or against a person in a representative capacity and there is a devolution of the interest of the representative, the rule that has to be applied is Order 22, rule 10 of Civil Procedure. [490 B C] 2. The word 'interest ' which is mentioned in this rule means interest in the property i.e., the subject matter of the suit and the interest is the interest or for any other reason. Order 22 rule 10 is not confined to devolution of interest of a party by death, it also applies if the head of the mutt or manager of the temple resigns his office or is removed from office. In such a case the successor to the head 'of the mut tiff or to the manager of a temple may be substituted as a party under this rule. [489 C D] 3. The fact that it was after Som Dass died that Shiam Dass was elected to be Mahant of Dera, and the appellant was elected as mahant of the office of Mahant in Patiala State, does not make any difference when the period of limitation for impleading them had expired. [488 E F] 4. In the instant case, the suit against Som Dass was filed by the respondent on the footing that the plaintiff as the legally appointed mahants were his lawfully appointed M. The appellant could not be added as parties under Order 22 Rule 10 of C.P.C. because he was elected in his capacity as a person who claimed to represent the dera as mahants of the defendant. [486 F G] 5. The question whether the interest in Dera was adverse to the respondent or that the suit was for possession and management of the property appertaining to it by the appellant purporting to be his successor was not raised before the High court. The High Court was right in holding that after death of the plaintiff, Shiam Das was sued in his place. [487 B C].

The Andhra Pradesh State Electricity Board, which was a statutory body constituted under the Andhra Pradesh Electricity Supply Act, 1948, framed regulations called the Hyderabad Civil Services Rules for the purpose of granting age of retirement to all Government employees other than in the last grade service. The Regulations were amended by the Andhra pradesh Electricity (Supply) Amendment Regulation No. 1 of 1979. By this amendment, the age of superannuation was raised from 55 to 58 years with effect from October 29, 1979 after an elaborate and scientific inquiry by a committee appointed by the Government of Andhra Pradesh. The age of retire ment was increased from 55 years to 58. In the writ petitions filed before the High Court, the petitioners contended that the amendment made in 1979 was bad because it had become necessary to provide greater employment opportunities to the youths who had already attained the age Of 55 years on February 8, 1983; and that the age should be raised from 60 to 58 only for the Central Government employees. The High Court rejected the contention of the petitioners. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the amendments were bad because they did not give any opportunity to the employees to file their writ petitions. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The amendment made by the impugned Regulation No 1 of 1980 in 1979 to the Fundamental Rules was valid and the power to amend these rules carries with it the power of the rule making authority or the Legislature. By that amendment, a proviso was added to Rule 2 which reads thus: "Provided that the rules shall not be modified or E; replaced to the disadvantage of any person already in service". The amendment was made by an amendment which was later on amended and substituted for the original clause (1) of Article 313 of the Constitution. [608C D] 1.2 The amendment of 1979 made in 1980, by which the age was raised to 58, was a valid exercise of legislative power. The rules and amendments made under the proviso to Article 309 can be altered or repealed by the Legislature but until that is done, the exercise of the power cannot be challenged as lacking in authority. There will be no order as to costs. [508D E] 1:3. The amendment to the rule made to the effect that the retirement age should continue to be 58 years for all services pensionable and non pensionable with an option to the Government to retire an employee on the ground of loss of efficiency, at the age not being a workman and not belonging to the last Grade Service shall retire from service on the afternoon of the last day of the month in which he attains the last date of the months in which the employee attains the age. [595C D; F] 1 :4. The proviso to Rule I of 1980, which conferred a benefit upon Government servants by protecting their conditions of service, cannot be amended so as to empower the Government or its authority to alter those conditions to their prejudice and, in any event, they cannot be amend retrospectively so as not to take away rights which had already accrued to them. [596E F] The amendment sought to be made by Rule 2 was a proper exercise of judicial power. It could not be said that the decision to reduce the age to 55 years was arbitrary or irrational and hence violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitu tion. [597F G] 1 5. The rule making power of Government is subject to judicial review. The power to alter the conditions of retirement from 58 to 55 is a valid power. [599H; 600A] 6. The amended proviso to rule 2 was deleted retrospectively, but it was made under an erroneous impression that it was not backed by due investigation or by compilation of relevant data on the subject. It was also made clear that the Government had exercised its power arbitrarily without any enquiry or by the compilation of rele vant data on that subject. [600E F; 600B] 7.

The appellants are dealers in raw materials in the State of Haryana. They purchased raw materials inside the State and exported those goods out of India. The respondent assessee purchased raw material inside the state from outside the State but paid no tax thereon, as they were registered dealers and furnished the declaration forms prescribed under section 24(1)(b) of the Haryana General Sales Tax Act, 1973. The assessing authority assessed the appellant to sales tax on the raw materials imposed under section 9(1) of that Act. This claim was rejected by the taxing authorities and the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants that: (i) the words "in the course of export outside India" in section 5(1), are used in the context of sales falling under sub section (3) but not under sub s.(1) thereof, and (ii) the expression "disposes of" used in clause (a)(ii) later on, clause (b) is used in relation to a sale or purchase within the meaning of section 5 of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The words "for the purpose of export" in sub s(1). are used with reference to sales and purchases that form part of his taxable turnover. This definition includes within the definition of 'turnover ' the purchase value of goods liable to tax under section 5 but the goods presently in question are not exigible to tax. [353B] 2. The expression "for sale" is defined in section 2(c) as meaning "the taking out of the goods from the State to any place outside it otherwise than by way of sale in the course oY of inter state trade or commerce". [353D] 3. The word "export" has been used in section 4(1 ) and not in sub section 2 (c). The expression 'sale proceeds of goods on which purchase tax is leviable under this Act ' means the taking out from the state to any places outside it, otherwise than in the way prescribed by section 5. [354E] 4. The language of section 9 (1) (a) and (b), as amended, is clear and unambiguous. It uses the words 'within the meaning ' in sub sec tion (1). The words 'in the case of goods which are not specified in Schedule B ' mean "the take out of tho goods specified in schedule B" but not in the form of a sale in that category. [355F] 5. The definition of "turnover" in Section 2(p) of section 2 is inclusive and includes within it, the taking Out of the taxable turnover under section 15, is only imposed on the sales and purchase price of any goods on the sale of which tax is levied under this act though the assessees are exempt from payment of such tax by reason of section 24 (1), [355G] 6. The Explanation to sub sec.(1). provides that a dealer registered under this section shall also be entitled to purchase, without payment of sales tax, at the rate notified under section 3, "the purchase value" of any 'goods on the Sales Tax Appeal No. 894/76 dated 31.3.1983 and the purchase price in the case the goods are specified in the Schedule B. The proviso thereto provides that where a dealer who purchases goods without payment or otherwise than under sub sec. (1)(a) of s 5, he shall be liable to pay tax on such sale at the rates notified under Section 15(3). [355H; 355A] 7. The explanation to section 9 of the Punjab General Sales tax Act, 1948 provides that "the sale proceeds of any good leviable under the Act" shall not include the purchase goods, that form parts of his gross turnover are included in Schedule A and that he is liable to be taxed on the purchases effected by him but for a claim for exemption under section 25.

The appellant firm was registered under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932. The goods were sent to the sellers by the sellers on board the ship and they were delivered to the buyers on board. The sellers returned the goods to the seller on the ground that these sales were not their property till the goods had crossed the customs barrier and thus entered the export stream. The Sales Tax Officer rejected the claim for exemption and assessed them to purchase tax under section 10(b) of the Bombay Sales Tax Act on the grounds that they remained the sellers ' property till they were brought on board and so the sales were exempted from tax under article 286(1)(b). The appellant 's appeal was dismissed by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. In further appeals to the Tribunal, the High Court held that the goods remained the seller 's property till after they had crossed customs barrier, and that therefore the exemption under article286(1) will come into operation. Held, that the words " a person " in section 10 (b) are wide enough to include a registered dealer and an unregistered dealer. The words " the time of the export" mean the time when the goods cross the customs frontier. The word " a registered dealers" is wide enough and includes a registered firm. In the United Motors case, the goods were on shipped by the seller and the contract was that payment will be made on the presentation of the bill of lading. The contract being that payment would be made at the time the goods reached the destination, the purchasing dealer had the intention as stated and ultimately he sold to a registered person. The fact remains that the intention declared has not been carried out. Held further, that in view of the provisions of section 10 of the Act no purchase tax was leviable from them under article 285(1).

The respondent wife married the appellant 's second wife. She was a second wife and had a son by her. The first wife died in 1956. A suit relating to a flat in which the husband had housed the wife resulted in a consent decree which also settled the marital disputes. The respondent filed an application for maintenance under section 125 of the Criminal Procedure Code, 1973 against the appellant and his father. The Magistrate found that the appellant was a subsisting wife and awarded monthly maintenance of Rs. 300/ . The High Court dismissed the revision petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the courts below had overlooked the plain provision in the Explanation (b) to section 125(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure which provides that the woman has been divorced by or has obtained a divorce from her husband and has not remarried. On behalf of respondent it was submitted that there must be proof of neglect to maintain to attract s.125 and his third contention was that there should be proof for maintenance. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellant 'S.127 rescue the respondent from his obligation. Payment of mehar money as a customary discharge is within the cognisance of that provision. But what was the amount of mehari ? Rs. 5000/ , interest from which could not keep the woman 's body and soul together for a day, even in that city where 40% of the population are reported to live on pavements, unless she was ready to sell her body and give up her soul. The husband has not examined himself to prove that he had been giving allowances to the divorced wife. His case is that she has forfeited her claim because of divorce and the consent decree does not have the special statutory right of the divorcee under section 127(3) of Cr. P.C. [79 C D] 2. The expression "in which a marriage otherwise eligible, is entitled" in section 125 means a woman who has been divorcee by or had obtained a decree from her court and has neither claimed nor remarried". It does not mean that the husband orders her out of the conjugal home. If law has nexus with life this argument is still born. The last defence based on mehar payment, merits more serious attention. [80 E F] 3. The consent decree of 1962 resolved all disputes and settled all claims then available but here is a new statutory right created as a projection of public policy by the Code. [81 G H] 4. If one were to locate a legal ground to raise the contention that the wife was not living separately by mutual consent, the court has spoken nothing to the contrary; and The High court has not spoken at all. Moreover, the husband has failed to prove his right to ignore the payment of the sum stipulated by customary or personal law whose quantum is more or less sufficient to do duty for maintenance allowance. [82 C D].

The Collector of the district after perusal of the office note passed order on 25th March, 1988 under which he was directed to black list the appellant. The said order was challenged by the State Government in a writ petition before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the black listing of the appellant was not specifically mentioned in the order and that there was no requirement for giving any prior notice before black listing any person. In this appeal, it was contended on behalf of the State that there is no requirement specifically of giving any notice under the rule of giving an opportunity to the appellant as he had been given a show cause notice and that the cancellation of the bid of the appel lant was not justified. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The black listing order passed by the Collector is set aside. So far as the cancellation is concerned, that is not affected. This order will, however, not prevent the State Govt. or the appropriate authorities from taking any future steps for cancelling the appellant if the Government is so entitled to do so in accordance with law. [868C D] 1.2 The order of the Collector dated 25th 3 1988 is set out in verbatim below: "Shri Raghu Nath Thakur S/o Late Gorakh Thakur, Village Repura, P.S. Puksha, District Samastipur has bid for Rs.11,900 (Rupees eleven thousands only) per month Dak in an auction held on 27.3.88 and he as given the shop of Beni Country liquor but after signing in Bandobasti Register he did not deposit dak amount. The name of Shri Raghu Nath Singh S/O Late Gorakh Nath Village Repudwara, Pages. 1.3 The cancellation of bid of appellant is concerned. That is not effected. [886D E] 2. The order dated 25.3 1988 of the Collec tor is set quashed. So long as the rules do not express so, it is an elementary principle of natural justice that parties affected by any order should have right of being heard and making representations against the order. In that view of the matter, the last portion of the order in so far as it directs black listing the appellant in respect of future contracts cannot be sustained in law.

The appellant landlord filed a suit for eviction of the respondent tenant on the ground that he was the landlord of the premises. The Rent Controller held that the building on the land leased to the respondent was not a vacant site and therefore, the claim in the suit for arrears of rent based on the rent controller 's order in respect of the said premises also could not be entertained. The appellant tenant filed an appeal against the order of eviction before the Rent Control Tribunal which held that since the subject matter of the lease under exhibit P 1 had been only a vacant land, the Rent Controller had no jurisdiction to entertain the application for fixation of fair rent in respect thereof and that therefore the claim of the appellant was not barred by section 12(4) of the Act. The Appellate Authority dismissed the appeal holding that the Rent controller had no jurisdic tion to entertain an application for fixing fair rent under section 4 of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948. On a reference made at the instance of the landlord, the High Court held that exhibit P1 was only a temporary piece of land and not a building site and that the claim by the appellant that he had decided to evict the respondent in the eviction petition under section 14(2)(vii) of Act was not correct. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the tenant that since exhibit PI was a lease agreement, the rent Controller had jurisdiction to determine the fair rent and that, therefore, it was open to the Rent Authority to go into the question of title in view of the decision in the first set of proceedings. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that exhibit PWI was not open to challenge on the grounds of title. [562D] 2. Section 4 of Tamil Nadu Act is a statutory jurisdiction which is vested in the Rent control ler by the terms of the Rent Act. It is an enabling provision which is available only for a vacant piece of lands and not of both land and buildings. The provisions of section 4 are intended to provide for a machinery for recovery of the amount. [563D] 3. Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides that where the Controller, on the language of section 5, has no jurisdiction in respect or other matters relating to the claim for arrears, he shall have power to entertain a suit by the defeated party and pass a decree for evic tion on any of the grounds mentioned in the said sections. The jurisdiction of the Civil Court is not barred under section 12 (4) from examining a claim of title merely because the question may have had to be considered by the Rent Tribunal as a collateral issue in deciding certain applications before them. [564D E] 4. Section 10(2) makes it clear beyond doubt that the Court of Small Causes is not competent to adjudicate on questions of title, and if the Civil court in this case had come to the conclusion that there was a relationship of landlord and tenant and that he has no title, yet, it would be open to him to seek eviction by having his title adjudicated upon in a civil court but that the owner cannot have a similar right in the matter of recovery of rent which is basically a relief for which he has to approach a civil Court. [565E F] 5. The question whether there is relationship of a landlord and a tenant and the land is not covered by section 10(1) or section 12, is only the determination as to the fair or standard rent of the land. If the Civil Courts in this respect are satisfied that there is a relationship between the parties, the landlord steps in for a limited purpose to determine what the fair and standard rent is and then fades out of the picture. Where a fair rent is fixed by a Controller, the Court has jurisdiction to adjudicate upon such matters as are not dealt with or ousted. [568F G] 6.

The Mysore State Civil Service Integration Rules, 1960 provide for filing of objections against the preliminary provisional inter state seniority list. The appellant was given a reasonable opportunity to object to the final list. He filed an objection on behalf of Union of India that he was not heard after the final gradation list was prepared. The High Court held that the combined final gradation lists were provisional and directed the final lists to be prepared after hearing objections. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The appellant respondent was entitled to an opportunity to make a representation with regard to the two points urged by him before the final select list was published. [828 D] Shankariah 's case, ; , followed. (2) The High Courts were under the misapprehension that the case now before them was also governed by what was held by this Court in Shankaria 's Case. [827 E F] (3) The principle recognised in Shanka Ram vs State of Rajasthan, [1962] Supp. 2 S.C.R. 829, applied. (4) The judgment of the Mysore High Court was not correct and must be set aside. [826 G H] (5) The respondent was not entitled to have a say against the final provisional list published on an integrated seniority list, as it had been prepared without due regard to particular important points which had to be considered before finalisation. What is meant was that certain principles were applied in the preparation of the list. These principles are generally found in the rules or executive directions which are known to or are capable of being found out by the persons affected. When a provisional seniority fist is prepared, there is a possibility of some mistakes occurring about the facts of a case or in the application of those rules. It would therefore be quite fair to give a person affected an opportunity of being heard against the proposed fist before it is finalised so that any possible mistakes, either on facts relating to his particular case or of law in applying the rules governing seniority to those facts may be rectified. But once he has had that opportunity, it cannot possibly be said that he should have a further opportunity against even a final seniority list.[826 H 827 A B] (6) The petitioner respondent was given an opportunity before the Court on the analogy of Shankarias ' case and on a failure to appreciate the facts in the case.

The petitioners are partnership firm carrying on business of import of rough diamonds and export of cut and polished diamonds. The Import & Export Policy for the period April 1978 to March, 1988 was in force in 1985. In the year 1979 78, the import of raw diamonds was granted by the Export Houses, which were registered in accordance with the provisions of the Import & Exports (Control) Act, 1947. The petitioners submitted application for registration as Export Houses and for grant of Export House Certificate under the Import Policy 1978 79. The applications were rejected on the view that they had failed to diversify their export obligation as a condition for grant or renewal of licence in the Import and Export Policy 197879. The petitioner filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the rejection of the application. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that sub para (10) of para 218 of the Policy eligibility for grant Of Export House Certificates was not only prohibited from importing items which were excluded under the Export Policy, but also from importing articles which were specifically banned altogether as well as items which are banned altogether. Dismissing the appeals, this Court HELD: 1. The licences issued to the Trading Houses and Export Houses prior to April 1, 1988 cannot be said to be persons similarly circumstanced as Export House who exported goods in the year 1987 88 and in subsequent years and obtain Additional Licences for a much lesser value under the import Policy 1978 91 on the basis of their exports during that period 1987 88. [244E] 2. The provisions conferring flexibility in the matter of imports contained in sub para.(4) of Para 215 of the Imports & Exports Policy 1988 91 are intended to give an incentive to Export Houses to increase the export prices of goods which appeared in Appendix 1 Part B of Import Policy 198891 on the ground that the conditions for grant and value of licences under the said clauses are quite different from those contained in the import and Export policy 1988 91. [243F] 3. The licence issued in favour of M/s. A.J.S.R.T. was valid for a period of twelve months and the said period has expired during the pendency of these writ petitions.[244G H; 244A] 4. The conditions for granting Additional licences are quite distinct from those mentioned in the Export & Import Policy, 1988 91, and so far as the Additional Licences were concerned, they are to be treated at par with Export Houses who have been granted Additional licences under that policy on the strength of their export licence. [245B] 5. The additional licences issued in pursuance of this Court 's order dated April 18, 1985 in Rajnikant Brothers case (supra) and had imported canalised items under the same import policy are quite separate from those covered by Appendices 1 to 215 of Appendix I Part B. [246D] 6. The Additional Licences issued to M/S. AJN & Co. (P) Ltd., cannot be held to be person similarly circumstanced. [247E] 7. The petitions are allowed and the orders passed by the High Courts are set aside.

The appellant is a division of McDowell & Co. Ltd., which has its factory at the material time in packed condition and the containers were not returnable by the buyer, and there fore, the goods were sold in bulk and delivered to customers at the appellant 's factory. The appellant had filed price lists in respect of the same. In respect of such consignments, the appellant was required to pay duty on the value of the drums manufactured by it. The Assistant Collector of Central Excise held that the goods are not returnable and hence the value could not be included in the assessable value. On appeal, the Appellate Tribunal held that at the time of removal, the good were delivered from the factory in packed conditions and the packing was not returnable to the buyer; there fore the value had to be included as per the definition of "value" in section 4(4)(d)(i) of the Act. The Revenue appealed to this Court by special leave against the order of the Tribunal. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The cost of packing contemplated in section 9(4) (d)(ii) of Central Excises & Salt Act, 1944 for determining the "value", in relation to any excisable goods is only the "cost of such packings" and not value. Therefore, it was held that where the Act provides for excise duty with reference to value of excisable goods, while determining the value, the cost of such packing would be includible in the value for assessment to excise duty. However, if any special secondary packing is provided by the assessee at the in stance of a wholesale buyer which is not generally provided as a normal feature of the wholesale trade, the costs of such special packing would not be includible. [995E F] 1.2 The cost incurred by the manufacturer and recovered by him from the purchaser whether as part of the sale price or separately, cannot be included under section 4 (4)(a) of Act. [996F G] 1:3. In construing section 4 of the Central Excises and Salt Act it is necessary to bear in mind that the measure of excise duty is price and not the value. The nature of the other payments referred to in sub clause (ii) all these show beyond doubt that while generally the normal price for which the goods arc sold at the factory gate is to be taken as the assessablevalue, an addition thereto has to be made where, in addition to the price, the manufacturer levies a charge for the packing which is intrinsically and inevitably incidental to placing the manufactured goods on the market.

The appellant was an Accountant cum Head Clerk in the Tamil Nadu Forest Training School at Vaigai Dam. He took charge of the office on 6.10.1975 and had been residing in a house opposite the training school. The appellant was charged with having committed food in the canteen for two days and being dissatisfied discontinued his practice before the notice was issued to him. The prosecution case was that the appellant had taken food in a canteen for three days and he was demanding bribe of Rs. 100. On 21.10,1975, the appellant was alleged to have pressed the demand to PW 1. The Trial Court accepted the prosecution evidence and convicted the appellant under section 161 I.P.C. and section 336 5(2) read with section 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act. The High Court dismissed the appeal filed by the appellant. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. There is no conclusive evi dence to hold that the appel lant was guilty. It is not a case that there had been consistent explanation for the appellant in his possession as a money returned by PW 1, the cir cumstances of the case would probabalise this case of the appellant and the presumption, if any, arising under section 4 is rebutted and the conviction cannot therefore be sustained. [357B] 2. The evidence of PW 1 is clearly incon sistent with the transaction of loan or return of money by PW l. This Court observed that though the conviction under section 165 I.
