The appellant was the founder of a Sansthan. The Sansthan was formed by the Maharaj who had movable property of the value of Rs. 19,164/ and immovable properties of the said Sansthan. In the year of account 18,164 61 were purchased from the temple by one Vithal Rukhamai. The appellant 's father died in 1952. The widow of the Sansthan filed a suit for declaration that the Sansthan was not a public trust. The trial court held that the deity was a private property and not a private trust. On appeal the District Judge reversed the decision holding that the appellant was a public Trust within the meaning of section 2(13) of the Act and restored the order of the Charity Commissioner. The High Court in revision set aside the order passed by the District judge and held that it was a Public Trust under section 29 of the , and therefore the appellant 'was not a trustee. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The High court was not right in giving due importance to the admission of the constituted attorney Ramkrishna Deshpande. [523 B] (2) The expression "public trust" is a very important piece of evidence to show that a public temple is a private one. The expression in the recital that "you are free as the full owner thereof" does not convert the gift which is expressly in favour of the deity or Sansthan into that in favour Of an individual as private property. [525 C D] (3) The definition of public trust contained in section 2 (13) and section 2 1(14) respectively of the Indian Trusts Act, 1882, shows that the property has always been treated as trust property even by the Officer saints and the Adhikaris or the disciples who succeeded one after the other were not owners but trustees of the property. The definition is very wide in its application to a public charitable trust. [500 D E] (4) In view of the fact that the temple was dedicated for the Darshan by the appellant, the endowment was a religious endowment within the scope of section 29 and the High Court was right in holding that it had no appearance of any impediment or restriction in the matter of continuous worship by the public extending over a long period. [511 C D; 512 A] (5) The position and purpose for which the trust was created, the consistent manner in which the property had been dealt with or managed by those in charge, the manner inwhich the property was dealt with, or managed, by those who were entitled to worship at the shrine of the temple, the nature of devolution of the properties, are all important elements in determination of the question whether a property is a public religious endowment. [506 B C] (6) The fact that a person has been appointed as manager of a temple does not make him a private or a body of persons interested. It is not always possible to have all the features of a public character without the least interference or restriction from the Temple authorities, to foster maintenance of the worship the accretion to the trust property by way of grants from the State of gifts from outsiders inconsistent with the private nature of the trust, the character of devolution being that of a religious trust. Therefore, in this case all the above tests are fulfilled. [605 C D]. (7) The properties in question were endowed for the worship of the public and the same had been managed by the saint. The fact of endowment was not such as to convert the gifts which was expressly in favor of the appellant.

The appellant was the sole proprietor of a business carried on under the name and style of Indestro Marketing, Bombay. The income tax authorities issued notices to the appellant for payment of the assessed amount of tax. The appellant challenged the validity of the said notices by filing a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court held that section 46(2) of the Indian Income tax Act was violative of article 14 of the Constitution and that section 13 of the Bombay City Land Revenue Act, 1876 was void under article 13(1). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that section 16 of the Act had no application to the present case as the assessment proceedings had been started and the certificate issued by the Income tax Officer to the Additional Collector of Bombay was not a valid one. HELD: (i) The impugned law is based on a territorial classification having a reasonable nexus or correlation between that basis of classification and the object sought to be achieved by the Act. [903 D] (ii) Section 46(1) of Indian Income Tax Act, 1922, which authorises the Collector to make an order for recovery of arrears of land revenue, is void under Article 13(i). The assessment proceedings having been started, the assessee must be governed by section 13 as it originally stood and not by it as subsequently amended. [803 G] Bhikaji Narayan Dhakras vs The State of Madhya Pradesh, ; , followed. (iii) Section 16 of Bombay City land Revenue Act is a territorial basis which is based upon an intelligible differentia and the subjection for the purposes of the recovery of tax by virtue of section 46 (2) is founded on a geographical classification having no reasonable nexus with that object. [883 A B] Bhikji Narayan Dhakas vs The Collector of Malabar, ; and Bhikaji N Dhakras 's case, referred to. (iv) Section 13 of Bombay Act has no application as the assessments had been commenced and the certificates had been issued by Income tax officer to the additional Collector of the State.

The respondents were the owners of a Port Trust, who were employed in the Bombay Port Trust. The respondents were paid wages at the time of the initial appointment and the same was fixed at Rs. 10,000/ per month. The Trustees of the Port Trust claimed that under a scheme of 12hour shift with 8 hours ' work, overtime should be at least 3 hours if not 4 hours in the case of an adult, 9 hours ' working day. The Tribunal held that the respondents were entitled to a 12 hours ' shift and rejected their claim for a fixed period of rest. On appeal by special leave: Held, that on any single day the number of hours of work must not exceed 9 and together with the hours of rest the total period of work and rest should not go beyond 12 hours. The provisions of section 13(2) (c) read with section 13 (3) give an indication of what is meant by an interval of rest and give an impression of what was meant by the interval of time. The scheme of the compels the inclusion of an hour of rest in a normal working day because the total number of work hours in a week cannot go beyond 48. The workers are entitled to three hours ' overtime if required to work beyond the 9 hours on any day. In a 12 hour shift, the nine hours of duty on anyday can be spread over 10 days and the extra hours will necessarily be hours of the rest. The provision of section 15(2)(c) of the Act does not itself fix the hours for rest but only fixes the hours in case of a adult, and it is wrong to contend that the period of 9 hours must always include intervals of rest; and if there is difficulty in giving the intervals for rest in that manner on any particular day, it cannot be said that the interval for rest shall break up the hours.

The appellant was the tenant of a shop in the respondent Nagar Palika Ghaziabad. The accommodation was let out on June 25, 1976. The respondent filed an eviction petition against the appellant under section 13(1) (a) of the Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 for ejectment of the appellant from the premises before the trial court and objection was raised that as the shop was let only on June 26, 1976, the provisions of the Act would not apply to these proceedings in view of the fact that the premises were let out in June 1976 but as the assessment was made on October 1, 1976 the provisions under the Act were applicable to these premises. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that since the premises had been let out for the first time on June 30, 1976 and during the pendency of this matter the appellant tenant will be entitled to protection of the provisions contained in the Act. The appellate authority confirmed the order of the trial Court. In the second appeal before the High Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent that since there was no provision of section 39 and 40 of the Rent Act, the suit could not be decreed as the protection available under this Act would be available to the tenant. On behalf of respondent it was submitted that the rights of parties will be governed by the provisions in the present case and therefore a decree for eviction could only be passed on the date on which the first assessment was filed. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The right of the parties will have to be determined on the basis of the rights available to them on the dates of the suit, but in Vineet Kumar vs Mangal Sain Wadhera, ; , this Court held that if during the pendin g of proceedings in this Court there is an assessment made then the date of completion of the building, the date from which 10 years are to be computed will be the date when the first assess ment was filed and not subsequently. [165G H] 1.2 The right to evict a tenant has been provided for in this Act under section 20 clause (1) of section 2. Clause (2) of Section 2 provides that where any building is constructed substantially out of funds obtained by way of loan or advance from the State Government or the Life Insurance Corporation of India or a bank or a co operative society or the Uttar Pradesh Guarantee Corpora tion, such building shall be deemed to have been completed on the day on which completion thereof is reported to or otherwise recorded by the local authority having jurisdiction. [166A B] 1:3 The right under clause (2), except in the case of a building constructed substantially in demolished, has been expressly declared to be an existing building which has been wholly or substantially demolished. Clause 2(1)(a) provides that no suit shall be instituted for the eviction of a tenant from any building, to which the old Act did not apply, pending on the said date. [167C D] 1 :4 The right given under clause 2(2) is to the landlord who has constructed substantially and the entire building including the existing building shall continue to be in occupation of the landlord for which the new Act does not apply. [168E F] 2:1.

The respondent instituted a suit for ejectment of three persons, who were the tenants under the appellant, and the third was the thika tenant. The trial court held that the appellant had not been liable to ejectment in view of section 29 of the West Bengal Thika Tenancy Act, 1949, as amended by the West Benabari Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance, 1952, which came into force on February 28, 1949. The High Court dismissed the suit holding that the respondent was not liable to eject the appellant under section 3 of the Act as he was a thika tenants within the meaning of the said Act as it was finally amended by an Act of 1953. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) Section 29 of West Bengal Tenancy Act 1949, which is prospective only, provides that where a landlord wished to eject a thikka tenant after the date of commencement of the Ordinance or proceeding which might be before the commencement of any court or before a person deciding an appeal under section 27 of the Calcutta Thika Tenants ' Act, 1950 for the time being in force as the case may be, he had to consider whether any of the grounds specified in section 3 were available to him and if so, he did not have to file a suit but apply to the Controller for relief on the basis that the applicant was a Thiika tenant within the mean ing of the provisions of the Bengal Thiaka Tenancy Act. [179 D E] (ii) The High Courts had rightly held that sections 4 and 5 being prospective and as such inapplicable to pre Act suits, the landlord had to establish the existence of one of the ground specified in s.3 in order to succeed. There being no provision for transfer of pending suits and appeals, the court hearing the appeal would have to pass a decree for ejectment even if the defendant was a Thika tenant after taking into account section 3. [180 E F] Mahadeolal Kanodia vs Administrator General of West Bangalpur Municipality, ; , followed. (iii) The landlord had not established any of these grounds specified under s. 3 entitling him to eject his tenant. [181 G H] Maha Deolal vs AdministratorGeneral of WestBengal, ; and Mahadeholal Kanojodia vs Estate Officer, A.I.R. 1953 Cal. 829, approved. (iv) The provisions of section 4 and the Explanation to s.4 of the East Bengal Thikka Tenancy (Second Amendment) Act, 1952 have to be examined in the light of the object of the enactment of the 1949 Act. The language of sections 4 & 5 being retrospective only it could not apply to pre existing suits and proceedings which were pending on 21st October 1952 and not in February 1949 i.e. the date when the commencement thereof or proceeding was commenced on the date on which the Act came into operation. [182 B C] Mahasudeol Kanodia, vs Administrator Gener al of West Calcutta, ; followed.

The State Government appointed a Pay Commission to examine the duties and responsibilities of different categories of posts. The Committee recommended for them a pay scale of Rs.200 400 as against Rs.120400. The State Government accepted the recommendations and issued an order dated July 2, 1976 appointing the Pay Commission (Amendment) 1971. The High Court took the view that the post of Bench Secretaries Grade I was not equivalent to Private Secretary in the scale of pay and that it should be treated as a superior class. In appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The principle of equal pay for equal work has to be construed in the first place. It cannot be denied that often the difference is a matter of degree and that there is an element of value judgment by those who are charged with the administration in fixing the scales of pay. So long as such value judgment emphasise that equal payfor equal work is a concomitant of Article 14 of the Constitution. But it follows naturally that equal pays for unequal work will be a negation of that right. And said: 1.(i) The principle is not expressly declared by this Constitution to be a fundamental right. [302E F] Randhir Singh vs Union of India, ; , referred to. (ii) The principles of equal Pay for equal Work have to be interpreted in the context of Article 39(d) of the Constitu tion and the principle of "equal pay for Equal work" has to he construed in a first place, [302G] 1.(iii) The classification between the posts of 10 Bench Secretaries and Section Officers is performing over the years and indeed superior to section officers. The Commission, Grade I are selected by a Selection Committee. The selection is based on merit with due regard to seniority. They are selected among the lot of Bench Secretary Grade II.

The appellant companies were incorporated under the , in the erstwhile State of Madhya Pradesh. Respondent 1, a Government Company incorporated under section 65 of the Madhya Pradesh Nagar Tatha Gram Nivesh Adhiniyam, 1973, was constituted under the Madhya Bharat Municipalities Act, 1961. The appellant company entered into an agreement with the respondent 1 for the Korba and other facilities for the development of the area. The respondent 1 was to carry on its business in the Kor baivesh and was also to pay property tax. The Company agreed not to exercise its power of taxation or to impose any other charges on the assets and activities of the company under the Act of 1973 as amended from time to time or under any other law or rules framed thereunder. The company entered upon an agreement dated January 28, 1976 with the appellant company for the purpose of carrying out development and use of land in consideration of the Authority agreeing not to do so. The agreement was renewed from time lo time by another notification dated March 15, 1977. The Government of Madhya Bharat issued a notification under section 69(d) of the Act on February 21, 1977, declaring that the company was liable to pay tax for the years 1976 77 and 1977 78 in respect of the years 1975 77 and 1978 78 in the sum of Rs. 11,000 78 annually. The appellants filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the validity of the demand notices on the ground that no tax was leviable on its property since the company had been carrying on an industry under the authority of the Central Government within the meaning of section 2(a) of Act 1973 and therefore the provisions of the Land Tax Act were not applicable to it. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the appellant companies did not fall within the purview of the expression "under the Act" as they had been owned wholly by the Government of India, and that the provisions conferring powers of taxation under the said two Acts must be taken to have been incorporated in section 69 (d) with effect from April 1, 1976. The State appealed to this Court by special leave. Allowing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High court was right in holding that in the meeting of January 29, 1976 respondent 1 acted beyond his authority in entering into the agreement with appellant companies under which respondent 1 bound itself not to impose tax on its properties and activities. [14E] 1.2 In the instant case, the Central Act was primarily concerned with the development and regulation of declared industries and not with the ownership of industrial undertakings. It is in pursuance of this power that the State Legislature enacted the Act. The legislative field covered by Entry 23 of List II will pass on to Parliament by virtue of Entry 54, List I. But in order to 20 judge whether on that account the State legislature loses its competence to pass the Act, it is necessary to have regard to the object and purpose of that Act and to the relevant provisions thereof under which Special Area Development Authorities are given the power to tax lands and buildings within their jurisdiction. [15E F] 1:3 The State Legislature has the competence to enact the impugned law. It has no competence to legislate on the subject and it is not correct to say that the property tax provided for in the Act is beyond the legislative competence of the State. [16G H] 1 :4. The power conferred by the State Legis lature under Entry 24, List II is not in any manner defeated by the legitimate exercise of taxing power under section 68(d). It is true that on account of declaration contained in section 2 of the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act 1957, the legislative field covers the development, and regulation and develop the mines as envisaged by the Nationalisation Act. But it is true, that on the question of the validity or otherwise of the provisions and the Municipal Corporation Act, 1956, the State Government has the power under Entry 23, List III to legislate in respect thereof.

The appellant was granted a lease for a period exceeding one year in respect of certain slate quarries within his estate. The appellant applied to the Collector for confirmation of the lease and the Collector confirmed the lease. On appeal, the Board of Revenue refused to ratify the lease on the ground that it did not give three months ' notice to the appellant or provide him with a reasonable opportunity of being heard. The Board of revenue declined to raitate the lease but granted a certificate under section 20(1) of the Abolition Act. The question for determination was whether the termination of the appellant 's lease by the order dated December 27, 1955, was bad as it did neither give three month ' notice nor provided for any compensation as required by section 20 of the Act. Held, that the Board had no power to terminate the lease under r. 47 of the Mineral Concession Rules of 1949 and the Government could not cancel the lease merely because the appellant had a right to claim compensation only when his right was terminated by the Government under the second proviso to section 20 (1). A mining lease granted by a private person shall be subject to certain conditions therein specified. The first proviso to r. 46(2) of 'the Rules provides that no rights shall be created after July 1, 1945, for a further period than one year. The second proviso is not exhaustive and does not apply to the termination by the State Government under r, 47. A mining leases granted by private persons on or after July I, 1945 could only be terminated if the Government was satisfied that it was in the public interest that it should be terminated and that further, in such cases, compensation will be payable under section20(2). The second Proviso to r, 46(1), which provides for termination of leases by the lessee, did not apply as the lease was for a fixed period. A lease for an indefinite period could only have been validly terminated if it was for any reason beyond the notified date and in such case compensation would be payable even after that date. The third proviso to rule 46(i) did not govern the rights created before July 1. 1945, but only enabled the Government to exercise its right conferred on it by the second Proviso. A lessee could terminate his lease at its option and unconditionally under proviso (iii) that can be done only if it is in the open interest of the Government and that being the position, the Government must do some overt act to terminate such lease and it would be impossible for the Government either to comply with the conditions laid down in the third proviso or to give three calendar months notice. The effect of the second provisos was to make the rights conferred on the lessee by the first proviso absolute and not void.
